Kirby CMS Panel installation endpoint accessed from external IP (CVE-2026-54003) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the Kirby Panel installation URI (/panel/installation) that complete from a non-private source IP. On a production Kirby site with an admin already created, the install endpoint should never be reachable; an external hit indicates either a vulnerable pre-install state being probed or active exploitation of the Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP header-confusion bypass. Rationale: Article specifies the attack target is the Kirby Panel installation flow (canonical URI /panel/installation), exploitable only when the site has no admin yet and the reverse proxy supplies Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP. Any external POST/GET to the install endpoint on a production site is high-fidelity — the endpoint is functionally unreachable post-setup. Private-IP exclusion strips dev/staging noise.
ATT&CKT1190 T1656
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer performing genuine first-time site install from outside the corporate network
  • External vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys, Nuclei) probing /panel/installation as a CVE check
  • Internet-wide opportunistic scanning (Censys/Shodan crawlers) hitting the install URI on a freshly stood-up host
  • Migration or DR rebuild where the site is temporarily admin-less and admin connects from a remote IP
  • Pen-test / red-team reconnaissance against the property
Suppression filter
| where UA !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Nuclei", "masscan", "zgrab", "Censys", "InternetMeasurement") | where ClientIP !in (dynamic(["<known-scanner-IPs>", "<dev-admin-home-IP>"]))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the Kirby version of the targeted host (vulnerable: <=4.9.3 or 5.0.0-alpha.1 through 5.4.3). Check the HTTP response code — 200 on a POST to /panel/installation means the request was accepted; pair with site/accounts/ inventory to see if a new admin was actually written. Identify the source IP and resolve geo/ASN. Step 2 (contain): If admin creation succeeded, take the site offline, force-delete the rogue account directory under site/accounts/, rotate any secrets the rogue admin could have exfiltrated, and patch to Kirby 4.9.4 or 5.4.4. If only probing, block source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the source IP across all web logs for the prior 30 days — same actor may have probed multiple Kirby properties. Review reverse-proxy config to confirm whether Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP headers are being passed and the upstream Kirby version handles them correctly. Audit all internet-facing Kirby installs for unpatched versions.
// Defender Advanced Hunting has no native web-access-log table; this surfaces the post-install admin login from the host side as a proxy signal
let PanelHosts = DeviceInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where IsInternetFacing == true
    | distinct DeviceId, DeviceName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where DeviceId in (PanelHosts)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nginx","nginx.exe","httpd","httpd.exe","apache2","caddy","w3wp.exe","php-fpm","php-fpm.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Primary detection: Kirby Panel install endpoint hit from external IP
let KirbyInstallPaths = dynamic(["/panel/installation", "/panel/install", "/api/users"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(W3CIISLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where csUriStem has_any (KirbyInstallPaths)
  | where csMethod in ("POST","PUT","GET")
  | extend Src="W3CIIS", ClientIP=cIP, URI=csUriStem, Method=csMethod, Status=tostring(scStatus), UA=csUserAgent),
(AppServiceHTTPLogs
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where CsUriStem has_any (KirbyInstallPaths)
  | where CsMethod in ("POST","PUT","GET")
  | extend Src="AppService", ClientIP=CIp, URI=CsUriStem, Method=CsMethod, Status=tostring(ScStatus), UA=UserAgent),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where RequestURL has_any (KirbyInstallPaths)
  | where RequestMethod in ("POST","PUT","GET")
  | extend Src="CEF", ClientIP=SourceIP, URI=RequestURL, Method=RequestMethod, Status=tostring(EventOutcome), UA=RequestClientApplication)
| where isnotempty(ClientIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(ClientIP)) and ClientIP !startswith "127." and ClientIP != "::1"
| project TimeGenerated, Src, ClientIP, URI, Method, Status, UA
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kirby CMS admin account file created under site/accounts/ by web server process (CVE-2026-54003) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a new Kirby account file (index.php / .txt / .yml) under the site/accounts/ directory by a web-server runtime process (php-fpm, nginx, apache, w3wp). After initial site setup, Kirby account files are normally added via the authenticated Panel — a new account directory appearing under site/accounts/ outside of a planned admin onboarding indicates either CVE-2026-54003 exploitation or another path to writing account YAML. Rationale: Kill-chain phase 3 explicitly names site/accounts/ as the persistence artefact — Kirby stores account YAML under that directory and the install flow's only side effect is dropping a new admin file there. Constraining the writer to web-server runtime processes (php-fpm, nginx, etc.) eliminates legitimate file-management writes from sysadmins or backup tooling. This is the cleanest exploitation-success signal: it fires only when an account was actually written, not on probe attempts.
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1078.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine first-time admin account creation via the Kirby install flow (intended behaviour on freshly-provisioned sites)
  • Migration / backup restore where site/accounts/ is being repopulated from a snapshot
  • Developer using Kirby CLI (kirby command) under the web-server user to programmatically provision accounts
  • Bulk user import via a Kirby plugin run from a web request
  • Configuration management (Ansible / Salt) writing accounts as the web user during deployment
Suppression filter
| where ActorUsername !in ("deployment-bot","backup-svc") | where TargetFilePath !contains "/backup/" and TargetFilePath !contains "/restore/"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the new account YAML — check the role: field (admin is the dangerous case) and the user email. Correlate Timestamp ± 60s against web access logs for POSTs to /panel/installation from the same host to confirm the exploitation path. Verify Kirby version (vulnerable: <=4.9.3 or 5.0.0-alpha.1 through 5.4.3). Step 2 (contain): Delete the rogue account directory under site/accounts/, terminate any active Panel sessions, rotate site secrets and any admin API tokens the rogue account could have minted, then upgrade Kirby to 4.9.4 / 5.4.4. If reverse proxy is upstream, audit its config to ensure Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP are either stripped or trusted appropriately. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the web-server process PID to enumerate every file write in the same session — check site/content/ for tampered pages, site/plugins/ for malicious plugin drops, and /site/config/ for unauthorized config changes. Review subsequent Panel/API auth events for the new account's user ID 
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/site/accounts/", @"\site\accounts\")
| where FileName in~ ("index.php","user.txt","index.yml","index.yaml",".htpasswd") or FileName endswith ".php"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php","nginx","nginx.exe","httpd","httpd.exe","apache2","w3wp.exe","caddy")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/site/accounts/", @"\site\accounts\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("index.php","user.txt","index.yml","index.yaml",".htpasswd") or TargetFileName endswith ".php"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php","nginx","httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe","caddy")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a8ecbd9c049044ca4990a0e5960d19ce782a3b42d7763e9693d7c91ead24a0b7", "914da75a4ad6d70db856a2bc318d8828f28894622f017ee78d470b4794faafa6", "a5e448af73b0ff6b6fcfe6ef7808120e1fd7e5c4c9b4edd68e1c980e5ea3406b", "7099c33933716c00c1f4bdb0281c230b981c76b23d7d1c83abc6f58968267d54", "56d656d684077e7b3231393f5464447cdc8eea81b6415c5f010bc52f0c8cb317") or SHA1 in~ ("a8ecbd9c049044ca4990a0e5960d19ce782a3b42d7763e9693d7c91ead24a0b7", "914da75a4ad6d70db856a2bc318d8828f28894622f017ee78d470b4794faafa6", "a5e448af73b0ff6b6fcfe6ef7808120e1fd7e5c4c9b4edd68e1c980e5ea3406b", "7099c33933716c00c1f4bdb0281c230b981c76b23d7d1c83abc6f58968267d54", "56d656d684077e7b3231393f5464447cdc8eea81b6415c5f010bc52f0c8cb317") or MD5 in~ ("a8ecbd9c049044ca4990a0e5960d19ce782a3b42d7763e9693d7c91ead24a0b7", "914da75a4ad6d70db856a2bc318d8828f28894622f017ee78d470b4794faafa6", "a5e448af73b0ff6b6fcfe6ef7808120e1fd7e5c4c9b4edd68e1c980e5ea3406b", "7099c33933716c00c1f4bdb0281c230b981c76b23d7d1c83abc6f58968267d54", "56d656d684077e7b3231393f5464447cdc8eea81b6415c5f010bc52f0c8cb317")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a8ecbd9c049044ca4990a0e5960d19ce782a3b42d7763e9693d7c91ead24a0b7", "914da75a4ad6d70db856a2bc318d8828f28894622f017ee78d470b4794faafa6", "a5e448af73b0ff6b6fcfe6ef7808120e1fd7e5c4c9b4edd68e1c980e5ea3406b", "7099c33933716c00c1f4bdb0281c230b981c76b23d7d1c83abc6f58968267d54", "56d656d684077e7b3231393f5464447cdc8eea81b6415c5f010bc52f0c8cb317") or SHA1 in~ ("a8ecbd9c049044ca4990a0e5960d19ce782a3b42d7763e9693d7c91ead24a0b7", "914da75a4ad6d70db856a2bc318d8828f28894622f017ee78d470b4794faafa6", "a5e448af73b0ff6b6fcfe6ef7808120e1fd7e5c4c9b4edd68e1c980e5ea3406b", "7099c33933716c00c1f4bdb0281c230b981c76b23d7d1c83abc6f58968267d54", "56d656d684077e7b3231393f5464447cdc8eea81b6415c5f010bc52f0c8cb317") or MD5 in~ ("a8ecbd9c049044ca4990a0e5960d19ce782a3b42d7763e9693d7c91ead24a0b7", "914da75a4ad6d70db856a2bc318d8828f28894622f017ee78d470b4794faafa6", "a5e448af73b0ff6b6fcfe6ef7808120e1fd7e5c4c9b4edd68e1c980e5ea3406b", "7099c33933716c00c1f4bdb0281c230b981c76b23d7d1c83abc6f58968267d54", "56d656d684077e7b3231393f5464447cdc8eea81b6415c5f010bc52f0c8cb317")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a8ecbd9c049044ca4990a0e5960d19ce782a3b42d7763e9693d7c91ead24a0b7", "914da75a4ad6d70db856a2bc318d8828f28894622f017ee78d470b4794faafa6", "a5e448af73b0ff6b6fcfe6ef7808120e1fd7e5c4c9b4edd68e1c980e5ea3406b", "7099c33933716c00c1f4bdb0281c230b981c76b23d7d1c83abc6f58968267d54", "56d656d684077e7b3231393f5464447cdc8eea81b6415c5f010bc52f0c8cb317"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hackers Abuse Claude.ai Shared Chat Feature to Host the ClickFix Social Engineering Instructions

Cyber Security News
2026-06-18 3 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

Hackers are increasingly exploiting trusted AI platforms to deliver sophisticated social engineering attacks, with a recent campaign abusing Claude.ai’s shared chat feature to host malicious ClickFix instructions. According to TrendAI Research, attackers deployed 106 unique malicious hostnames across six campaign waves within seven weeks, continuously rotating infrastructure and testing different AI-themed lures to maximize effectiveness. [&#8230;] The post Hackers Abuse Claude.ai Shared Chat Feature to Host the ClickFix Social Engineering Instructions appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Details Windows Clipper Malware Campaign Using USB LNK Worm and Tor-Based C2

The Hacker News
2026-06-18 9 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft has disclosed details of a Windows-based cryptocurrency clipper campaign that has targeted users since February 2026. "The clipper in this campaign relies on Windows Script Host and ActiveX-driven logic to launch a bundled Tor proxy and poll a hidden-service C2 [command-and-control] server," the Microsoft Defender Security Research Team said in an analysis published Tuesday. "It

ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1190 T1555.003

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] USB-borne LNK spawns wscript/cscript referencing removable drive path
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] WScript/CScript spawning curl, cmd, or PowerShell (Microsoft-recommended clipper signal) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Scheduled task registers wscript/cscript-launched payload for clipper persistence · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Local SOCKS5 listener on Tor-default port from non-browser binary (bundled Tor proxy) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PowerShell screen capture via System.Drawing CopyFromScreen (Microsoft clipper signal) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
USB-borne LNK spawns wscript/cscript referencing removable drive path AIDelivery High
Hunts the initial-access vector described by Microsoft: a user double-clicks a LNK file on a USB drive that mimics a hidden DOC/XLSX/PDF, causing explorer.exe to launch wscript.exe or cscript.exe with arguments pointing at a removable-drive path. This is the worm's entry point before persistence is installed. Rationale: Article explicitly states the LNK files on USB carry 'arguments that line to the worm component' which the user launches thinking it is a hidden DOC/XLSX/PDF. The parent of a user-clicked LNK is explorer.exe; the child is wscript/cscript; the command line will reference the removable-drive path. Removable-drive letters typically fall in D:-Z: range and combine with .lnk/.vbs/.js extensions for very high fidelity.
ATT&CKT1091 T1204.001 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate VBS/JS deployment scripts run from network share mapped to drive letters E:/F:
  • IT admin testing autorun behaviour with benign scripts on USB
  • Document-management software auto-launching .vbs file-rename helpers
  • User-installed portable apps on USB drives that ship with .vbs launchers (PortableApps.com)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and identify the script path; check DeviceFileEvents on the source drive letter for hidden DOC/XLSX/PDF files with matching LNK siblings. Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response, eject and quarantine the USB device, dump the script body for sandbox analysis. Hunt: query DeviceProcessEvents across the fleet for the same script SHA256 over 30 days, look for scheduled-task creations referencing the same script path, and review DeviceNetworkEvents for any local-loopback SOCKS5 (9050/9150) listeners that may indicate the Tor proxy stage has already deployed.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)[D-Z]:\\"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any (".lnk",".vbs",".js",".vbe",".jse")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "explorer.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)[D-Z]:\\" or CommandLine has_any (".lnk",".vbs",".js",".vbe",".jse")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: USB LNK Worm Spawns Windows Script Host from Removable Drive
id: 8b9c0d4f-2e35-4a18-9c52-7a91b3f6d2c1
description: Detects explorer.exe spawning wscript.exe or cscript.exe with command-line referencing a removable-drive path (D:..Z:) or LNK/VBS/JS file, matching the Microsoft-reported USB LNK worm clipper campaign.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.t1091
  - attack.t1204.001
  - attack.t1059.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\explorer.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
  cmd_paths:
    CommandLine|re: '(?i)[D-Z]:\\\\'
  cmd_exts:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '.lnk'
      - '.vbs'
      - '.js'
      - '.vbe'
      - '.jse'
  condition: selection and (cmd_paths or cmd_exts)
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) @ParentImage:(*\\explorer.exe OR *\\EXPLORER.EXE OR *\\Explorer.exe) @Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\WSCRIPT.EXE OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe OR *\\CSCRIPT.EXE) @CommandLine:(*.lnk* OR *.vbs* OR *.js* OR *D\:\\* OR *E\:\\* OR *F\:\\* OR *G\:\\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/explorer\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)([D-Z]:\\\\|\\.lnk|\\.vbs|\\.js|\\.vbe|\\.jse)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name=explorer.exe Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") (Processes.process_path="*.lnk*" OR Processes.process="*.lnk*" OR Processes.process="*\\:*.vbs*" OR Processes.process="*\\:*.js*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)[D-Z]:\\\\")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name=explorer.exe Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") (Processes.process_path="*.lnk*" OR Processes.process="*.lnk*" OR Processes.process="*\\:*.vbs*" OR Processes.process="*\\:*.js*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)[D-Z]:\\\\")
WScript/CScript spawning curl, cmd, or PowerShell (Microsoft-recommended clipper signal) AIExploitation High
Hunts the execution chain Microsoft explicitly recommended defenders watch for: wscript.exe or cscript.exe launching curl, cmd.exe, PowerShell, or unexpected executables. This is the clipper's ActiveXObject-driven WScript code reaching out to fetch payloads or invoke its bundled Tor proxy. Rationale: Direct quote from Microsoft in the article: defenders should look for 'use of WScript, CScript, or related script engines for launching curl, cmd.exe, PowerShell, or unexpected executables.' The clipper's ActiveXObject design routes everything through WScript, so this parent/child relationship is the canonical execution fingerprint.
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy enterprise VBScript admin tooling that shells out to PowerShell for system queries
  • SCCM/Intune deployment wrappers that chain VBS to cmd.exe for legacy installer logic
  • Citrix logon scripts invoking certutil for cert pinning
  • Internal IT helpdesk scripts using cscript-driven cmd.exe wrappers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\System32\\CCM\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Microsoft Intune Management Extension\\"
Response runbook
Triage: extract the parent script path and full ChildCmd; pull the script content from disk (if still present) for sandbox analysis. Contain: kill the parent script process tree, isolate the host, and block the script SHA256 via Defender custom IOC. Hunt: query DeviceNetworkEvents for the parent script process making outbound connections to .onion-style infrastructure or to localhost SOCKS5 ports (9050/9150), and look for AsepValueUpdate registry persistence written by the same wscript/cscript instance.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","wget.exe","mshta.exe","regsvr32.exe","rundll32.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentScript = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentFolder = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ChildProcess = FileName,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("curl.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","wget.exe","mshta.exe","regsvr32.exe","rundll32.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Scheduled task registers wscript/cscript-launched payload for clipper persistence AIInstallation High
Detects the worm component installing scheduled-task persistence for itself and the clipper, as described in the article. Looks for schtasks.exe creating tasks whose action invokes wscript.exe or cscript.exe with a user-writable path (Temp, AppData, ProgramData, Public). Rationale: Article: 'The worm component … deploys scheduled tasks as a form of persistence for both the worm component and the stealer component.' The clipper uses WScript/ActiveXObject so any installed task action will reference wscript or cscript pointing at a payload outside Program Files — that combination is rarely benign.
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate enterprise login-banner script deployed via scheduled task pointing to ProgramData
  • Software-vendor uninstaller cleanup tasks shipping VBS in %ProgramData%\<Vendor>\
  • Adobe/Java updater registered as scheduled-task VBS hooks
  • IT-admin ad-hoc tasks running diagnostic VBS from a user profile path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\System32\\CCM\\" and ProcessCommandLine !has "\\Program Files\\"
Response runbook
Triage: extract task name and the full TR (task-run) argument from the command line; pull the referenced script for sandbox analysis. Contain: delete the scheduled task with schtasks /Delete /F, kill any running instances, and isolate the host. Hunt: query DeviceEvents for ActionType=ScheduledTaskCreated across the fleet for the same script SHA256 or task name, and check DeviceFileEvents for the original payload file to identify the delivery vector (USB drive letter or download URL).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/Create","/CREATE")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wscript","cscript")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\AppData\\","\\Temp\\","\\ProgramData\\","\\Public\\","\\Users\\Public\\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/Create","/CREATE")
| where CommandLine has_any ("wscript","cscript")
| where CommandLine has_any ("\\AppData\\","\\Temp\\","\\ProgramData\\","\\Public\\","\\Users\\Public\\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Schtasks Registers WScript Or CScript Payload From User-Writable Path
id: 5f2b9c41-7d18-4a93-91be-3e95ad6c4d22
description: Detects schtasks.exe creating a scheduled task whose action invokes wscript.exe or cscript.exe against a payload in a user-writable directory, matching the Microsoft-reported clipper persistence step.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/18
tags:

  - attack.t1547
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/Create'
      - '/CREATE'
  script_engine:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'wscript'
      - 'cscript'
  user_writable:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '\AppData\'
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
      - '\Public\'
      - '\Users\Public\'
  condition: selection and script_engine and user_writable
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:((*Create* OR *CREATE*) AND (*wscript* OR *cscript* OR *WScript* OR *CScript*) AND (*AppData* OR *Temp* OR *ProgramData* OR *Public*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/schtasks\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)/create", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)(wscript|cscript)", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)\\\\(AppData|Temp|ProgramData|Public|Users\\\\Public)\\\\", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())

Local SOCKS5 listener on Tor-default port from non-browser binary (bundled Tor proxy) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the bundled Tor client described in the article: a renamed Tor binary opening a local SOCKS5 listener on the default Tor ports (9050/9150) from a process that is not Tor Browser, Brave, or another known Tor-aware app. The clipper routes C2 through this local proxy, so the listener is a strong signal. Rationale: Article states the malware 'launches a renamed Tor binary in a hidden window' and 'routes traffic through a local SOCKS5 proxy.' Tor's default SOCKS5 ports are 9050 (tor.exe) and 9150 (Tor Browser). A loopback connection or listener on those ports from a process that is NOT a known Tor client is exactly the renamed-Tor signature the article describes.
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1572 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using Tor SOCKS proxy via a custom Python script for legitimate research
  • Privacy-tool users running Tor via OnionShare or BridgeRelay portables under a renamed wrapper
  • Penetration-tester using torsocks during an authorised engagement
  • Anonymisation-aware crypto wallet apps (e.g. Wasabi, Samourai) that ship their own SOCKS5 binding
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Tor Browser\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\OnionShare\\"
Response runbook
Triage: identify the binding process via InitiatingProcessSHA256 and InitiatingProcessFolderPath; submit hash to threat intel and inspect the on-disk binary for Tor strings/imports despite the renamed filename. Contain: kill the proxy process, isolate the host, capture memory if possible, then quarantine the binary. Hunt: query DeviceProcessEvents for the same SHA256 across the fleet, check DeviceRegistryEvents and scheduled-task creations referencing the same path, and look at DeviceFileEvents for any .onion-related config files (torrc) dropped to %AppData% or %ProgramData%.
let TorPorts = dynamic([9050, 9150]);
let KnownTorClients = dynamic(["tor.exe","firefox.exe","tor-browser.exe","brave.exe","torbrowser.exe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","ListeningConnectionCreated")
| where RemotePort in (TorPorts) or LocalPort in (TorPorts)
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or LocalIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (KnownTorClients)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256,
          LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
let TorPorts = dynamic([9050, 9150]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber in (TorPorts) or SrcPortNumber in (TorPorts)
| where DstIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or SrcIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcPortNumber, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationPort:9050 OR @DestinationPort:9150) @DestinationIp:(127.0.0.1 OR \:\:1) -@Image:(*\\tor.exe OR *\\Tor.exe OR *\\TOR.EXE OR *\\firefox.exe OR *\\Firefox.exe OR *\\tor-browser.exe OR *\\brave.exe OR *\\Brave.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemotePort=9050 OR RemotePort=9150) RemoteAddressIP4=/^127\./
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/(tor|firefox|tor-browser|torbrowser|brave)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK

| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_port=9050 OR All_Traffic.dest_port=9150) (All_Traffic.dest_ip="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest_ip="::1") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where NOT (process_name IN ("tor.exe","firefox.exe","tor-browser.exe","brave.exe"))

PowerShell screen capture via System.Drawing CopyFromScreen (Microsoft clipper signal) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the clipper's screenshot-exfiltration stage. Microsoft's article explicitly recommends 'PowerShell-based screen capture' detection. The Bitmap/Graphics/CopyFromScreen API pattern is the canonical way PowerShell grabs the desktop and is rarely seen in benign workloads. Rationale: Direct Microsoft recommendation in the article: 'defenders prioritize behavioral detections … specifically looking for PowerShell-based screen capture.' The .NET System.Drawing classes with CopyFromScreen are the standard PowerShell screenshot pattern and the clipper does periodic screen-grab exfiltration over Tor — so the API string is the natural cmd-line fingerprint.
ATT&CKT1113 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal ITAM or RMM tool grabbing screenshots for endpoint inventory dashboards
  • Developer testing a screenshot-utility PowerShell module
  • Help-desk session-recording scripts using Bitmap APIs for incident capture
  • ScreenConnect/ConnectWise remote-support agents using PowerShell wrappers for thumbnails
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\ScreenConnect\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\ConnectWise\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\SCCM\\"
Response runbook
Triage: extract the full PowerShell command line, decode any inline base64 or compressed payload, identify the target output path (where the bitmap is written). Contain: kill the PowerShell process tree, isolate the host, and review %TEMP%/%APPDATA% for recently-written PNG/JPG/BMP files that may be queued for Tor upload. Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessFileName — if wscript.exe or cscript.exe is the parent, this is the clipper chain; query DeviceNetworkEvents for the parent process touching localhost:9050/9150 and pull any scheduled tasks that launch the same script.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("System.Drawing","CopyFromScreen","Drawing.Bitmap","Drawing.Graphics","FromImage","PrimaryScreen.Bounds")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("System.Drawing","CopyFromScreen","Drawing.Bitmap","Drawing.Graphics","FromImage","PrimaryScreen.Bounds")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PowerShell Screen Capture Via System.Drawing.CopyFromScreen
id: 9c4e1a72-6b08-4f15-bd83-2c47ed85a0f9
description: Detects PowerShell command lines that load System.Drawing and invoke CopyFromScreen / Bitmap / Graphics APIs to grab the desktop, matching Microsoft's explicit recommendation for the Tor-based clipper campaign.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") (Processes.process="*System.Drawing*" OR Processes.process="*CopyFromScreen*" OR Processes.process="*Drawing.Bitmap*" OR Processes.process="*Drawing.Graphics*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] GHSA-f38v-77qj-h4jq: praisonai-platform 0.1.4 still boots on t
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Vulnerable praisonai-platform server launch (GHSA-f38v-77qj-h4jq / CVE-2026-47410) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] praisonai-platform workspace-member enumeration fan-out (forged-JWT recon) · [LLM] praisonai-platform workspace / member destructive DELETE (forged-JWT impact)
Vulnerable praisonai-platform server launch (GHSA-f38v-77qj-h4jq / CVE-2026-47410) AIInstallation High
Detects Python/uvicorn launching the praisonai-platform FastAPI app, the documented entry points 'python -m praisonai_platform' and 'uvicorn praisonai_platform.api.app:app'. Versions <=0.1.4 sign/verify JWTs with the public literal 'dev-secret-change-me' whenever PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET is unset and PLATFORM_ENV defaults to 'dev', which is the unmodified default state of the package. Identifies exposed vulnerable instances before exploitation. Rationale: Article names the exact documented entry points: 'python -m praisonai_platform --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000' and 'uvicorn praisonai_platform.api.app:app --host 0.0.0.0' (auth_service.py path src/praisonai-platform/praisonai_platform/services/auth_service.py). Detecting these launches identifies vulnerable deployments since 0.1.4 == default-open. Cross-checked parent advisory GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 / CVE-2026-47410 confirming the hardcoded secret 'dev-secret-change-me' and that no shipped Dockerfile / compose sets PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/praisonai-platform/CVE-2026-47410/ • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-3qg8-5g3r-79v5
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running the server locally with PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET and PLATFORM_ENV=prod explicitly exported
  • CI/CD integration-test runner that spins up the package in an ephemeral container
  • QA staging host that is firewall-isolated from the public internet
  • Security researcher reproducing the PoC in a sandbox
  • Internal documentation/training environment
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has_any ("dev-", "staging-", "ci-", "build-", "qa-") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET="
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the host owner and confirm whether the instance is dev/test (allow-listed) or production-exposed. On the running PID, read `tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/<pid>/environ` and verify PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET is set to a strong random value (NOT 'dev-secret-change-me') AND PLATFORM_ENV != 'dev'. Step 2 (contain): If unset or default, export a fresh 32+ byte random PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET and restart — this invalidates every existing JWT (legit and forged). If internet-exposed, place behind authenticating reverse proxy or take offline until rotated; consider pinning a patched fork. Step 3 (hunt): Pull web-access logs for the host's listening port over the last 30 days for any DELETE on /workspaces/{uuid} or GET on /{uuid}/members and the source IPs/UAs; correlate against pre-rotation JWT subs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3","python3.exe","python","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe","gunicorn") or FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3","python3.exe","python","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe","gunicorn")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai_platform.api.app:app", "-m praisonai_platform", "praisonai_platform --host")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai_platform.api.app:app", "-m praisonai_platform", "praisonai_platform --host")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Vulnerable praisonai-platform Server Launch (GHSA-f38v-77qj-h4jq / CVE-2026-47410)
id: 4f8e3d2a-1c5b-4a6e-9f7a-3c2b1d8e4f5a
description: |
  Detects launch of the praisonai-platform FastAPI server. Versions <=0.1.4 sign and verify
  JWTs with the public default secret 'dev-secret-change-me' unless PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET is set
  AND PLATFORM_ENV != 'dev'. Default state is vulnerable; an unauthenticated attacker can forge
  a JWT for any user_id and take over workspace-owner accounts.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f38v-77qj-h4jq
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-47410
author: Detection-as-Code
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1078
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'praisonai_platform.api.app:app'
      - '-m praisonai_platform'
      - 'praisonai_platform --host'
  condition: selection_cmd
falsepositives:
  - Developer running the package locally with PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET / PLATFORM_ENV explicitly set
  - CI integration tests
level: medium
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:(*praisonai_platform.api.app:app* OR *praisonai_platform* OR *praisonai-platform*)) OR (source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*praisonai_platform.api.app:app* OR *"-m praisonai_platform"* OR *praisonai_platform*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| CommandLine=/praisonai_platform/i
| ImageFileName=/(python3?(\.exe)?|uvicorn|gunicorn)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*praisonai_platform.api.app:app*" OR Processes.process="*-m praisonai_platform*" OR Processes.process="*praisonai_platform --host*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*praisonai_platform.api.app:app*" OR Processes.process="*-m praisonai_platform*" OR Processes.process="*praisonai_platform --host*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
praisonai-platform workspace-member enumeration fan-out (forged-JWT recon) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for a single source IP or principal reading GET /{workspace_id}/members across many distinct workspaces in a short window. Per the article, this endpoint returns every member's user_id, which an attacker holding a forged JWT uses to identify workspace-owner user_ids before targeted owner impersonation. Threshold-based behavioural detection. Rationale: Article explicitly identifies GET /{workspace_id}/members as the discovery primitive that reveals workspace-owner user_ids ('returns List[MemberResponse], each carrying user_id and role, to any holder of require_workspace_member'). user_ids are uuid4 per the article so the UUID regex on the path component is tight. Fan-out (>=5 distinct workspaces from one src) is the high-fidelity signal — legit members read one workspace's members; attackers iterate. defender_kql empty: web access logs are not in Defender XDR tables. falcon_logscale_query empty: Falcon FDR does not ship HTTP URL paths from arbitrary applications. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5
ATT&CKT1087.004 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Workspace admin auditing members across many workspaces they own
  • Compliance/backup tool that periodically enumerates members for export
  • E2E test suite that creates many workspaces then lists their members
  • SSO provisioning sync agent reconciling membership
  • Customer-success rep helping users across many workspaces
Suppression filter
| where csUserName !in~ ("svc-praison-compliance", "svc-praison-backup", "svc-praison-provisioning") and csUserAgent !has_any ("praison-backup-agent", "compliance-scanner/")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Resolve cIP and csUserName to a human or service principal; check whether they legitimately own/admin the enumerated workspaces. Confirm the JWT 'sub' from the X-Authenticated-User / app log matches the expected csUserName. Step 2 (contain): If the principal isn't an authorised admin, immediately rotate PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET (invalidates all sessions), force re-auth, and block the source IP. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to DELETE actions on /workspaces/{id} or PATCH/PUT on /{id}/members/{user_id} from the same cIP / csUserName over the last 7d; check for newly-created admin members; look for the same fan-out pattern from other sources.
let UuidRe = @"^/[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}/members$";
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csMethod == "GET"
| where csUriStem matches regex UuidRe
| summarize WorkspacesEnumerated = dcount(csUriStem),
            FirstHit = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastHit  = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleAgent = any(csUserAgent),
            SampleStatus = any(scStatus),
            SampleWorkspaces = make_set(csUriStem, 10)
            by cIP, csUserName
| where WorkspacesEnumerated >= 5
| order by WorkspacesEnumerated desc
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:aws.alb) @http.method:GET @http.url_details.path:*/members
# log group: /aws/applicationelb (point at the ALB fronting praisonai-platform)
fields @timestamp, client.ip, request, elb_status_code, user_agent
| filter request like /GET https?:\/\/[^\/]+\/[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}\/members/
| stats count_distinct(request) as workspaces_enumerated, min(@timestamp) as first_seen, max(@timestamp) as last_seen by client.ip
| filter workspaces_enumerated >= 5
| sort workspaces_enumerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(Web.url) as workspaces_enumerated, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Web.user_agent) as user_agents, values(Web.url) as sample_urls from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method="GET" Web.url="*/members" Web.url="*-*-*-*-*/members" by Web.src Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where workspaces_enumerated >= 5 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Web.url) as workspaces_enumerated, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Web.user_agent) as user_agents, values(Web.url) as sample_urls from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method="GET" Web.url="*/members" Web.url="*-*-*-*-*/members" by Web.src Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where workspaces_enumerated >= 5 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
praisonai-platform workspace / member destructive DELETE (forged-JWT impact) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects DELETE requests on praisonai-platform's owner-gated destructive endpoints: DELETE /workspaces/{workspace_id} (wipes the workspace + every contained resource) and DELETE /{workspace_id}/members/{user_id} (evicts legitimate members). Per the article these are the irrecoverable A:H operations reachable via a forged JWT signed with the public default secret. Rationale: Article calls out the exact destructive routes: 'DELETE /workspaces/{workspace_id} (gated by require_workspace_owner), which deletes the entire workspace and every contained resource, and DELETE /{workspace_id}/members/{user_id}, which evicts legitimate members'. Both gated only by JWT 'sub' matching workspace_owner role, which the forged token satisfies. uuid4 path components yield tight regex anchors. Cross-checked sibling advisories GHSA-c2m8-4gcg-v22g (9.6) and GHSA-h8q5-cp56-rr65 (referenced) confirming the same routes. defender_kql empty: HTTP access logs are not in Defender XDR. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/praisonai-platform/CVE-2026-47410/
ATT&CKT1485 T1531 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate workspace owner deleting their own old/test workspace
  • Admin offboarding script evicting departed employees from member lists
  • E2E test teardown that creates and then deletes ephemeral workspaces
  • Customer-initiated account closure flow that cascades workspace delete
  • Bulk-cleanup job removing workspaces flagged for end-of-life
Suppression filter
| where csUserName !in~ ("svc-praison-admin", "svc-praison-offboarding") and not (csUserAgent has_any ("praison-e2e", "praison-cleanup-job") and sSiteName has_any ("staging", "test"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Snapshot the request — cIP, csUserName/JWT sub, scStatus, csUserAgent. Confirm with the workspace owner out-of-band whether they actually initiated the DELETE (if 2xx, the resource is already gone). Verify the deployment's PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET is not the default 'dev-secret-change-me'. Step 2 (contain): If unauthorised or the secret is default, immediately rotate PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET to a strong random value (invalidates all forged AND legit tokens — accept the user-impact tradeoff), force re-auth, block the source IP at WAF. Restore the workspace from the most recent backup. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all DELETE/PATCH on /workspaces/* and /*/members/* over the prior 30 days; correlate by source IP, csUserName, and JWT sub; check for orphaned workspaces that lost their owner; review GHSA-c2m8-4gcg-v22g and GHSA-h8q5-cp56-rr65 for related privilege paths.
let WorkspaceDel = @"^/workspaces/[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}$";
let MemberDel    = @"^/[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}/members/[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}$";
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csMethod == "DELETE"
| where csUriStem matches regex WorkspaceDel
   or  csUriStem matches regex MemberDel
| where scStatus startswith "2"          // succeeded
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csUserName, csMethod, csUriStem, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: praisonai-platform Destructive API Call (Workspace/Member DELETE - GHSA-f38v-77qj-h4jq)
id: 8a3e2c1b-7f4d-4e9a-b6c8-5d4e3f2a1b9c
description: |
  Detects DELETE on praisonai-platform /workspaces/{uuid} or /{uuid}/members/{uuid}.
  Given CVE-2026-47410 (JWT signed with public 'dev-secret-change-me'), any DELETE may
  originate from a forged token unless the deployment explicitly set PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f38v-77qj-h4jq
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5
author: Detection-as-Code
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1485
  - attack.t1531
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_workspace:
    cs-method: DELETE
    cs-uri-stem|re: '^/workspaces/[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}$'
  selection_member:
    cs-method: DELETE
    cs-uri-stem|re: '^/[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}/members/[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}$'
  condition: selection_workspace or selection_member
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate workspace owner deleting their own workspace
  - Admin offboarding script removing departed users
level: high
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:aws.alb) @http.method:DELETE (@http.url_details.path:/workspaces/* OR @http.url_details.path:*/members/*)
# log group: /aws/applicationelb (point at the ALB fronting praisonai-platform)
fields @timestamp, client.ip, request, elb_status_code, user_agent, target_status_code
| filter request like /DELETE https?:\/\/[^\/]+\/(workspaces\/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}|[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}\/members\/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36})/
| filter elb_status_code like /^2/
| sort @timestamp desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as urls values(Web.user_agent) as agents values(Web.status) as statuses from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method="DELETE" (Web.url="*/workspaces/*" OR Web.url="*/members/*") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where match(urls, "/workspaces/[0-9a-f-]{36}") OR match(urls, "/[0-9a-f-]{36}/members/[0-9a-f-]{36}") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as urls values(Web.user_agent) as agents values(Web.status) as statuses from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method="DELETE" (Web.url="*/workspaces/*" OR Web.url="*/members/*") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where match(urls, "/workspaces/[0-9a-f-]{36}") OR match(urls, "/[0-9a-f-]{36}/members/[0-9a-f-]{36}") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("cc29d43c5412da2c73c818859b8d8b146587842999b777336017ab9d9e509258", "8acf77c531e624c46d3d61dcae37e9942e90972c") or SHA1 in~ ("cc29d43c5412da2c73c818859b8d8b146587842999b777336017ab9d9e509258", "8acf77c531e624c46d3d61dcae37e9942e90972c") or MD5 in~ ("cc29d43c5412da2c73c818859b8d8b146587842999b777336017ab9d9e509258", "8acf77c531e624c46d3d61dcae37e9942e90972c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("cc29d43c5412da2c73c818859b8d8b146587842999b777336017ab9d9e509258", "8acf77c531e624c46d3d61dcae37e9942e90972c") or SHA1 in~ ("cc29d43c5412da2c73c818859b8d8b146587842999b777336017ab9d9e509258", "8acf77c531e624c46d3d61dcae37e9942e90972c") or MD5 in~ ("cc29d43c5412da2c73c818859b8d8b146587842999b777336017ab9d9e509258", "8acf77c531e624c46d3d61dcae37e9942e90972c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["cc29d43c5412da2c73c818859b8d8b146587842999b777336017ab9d9e509258", "8acf77c531e624c46d3d61dcae37e9942e90972c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PraisonAI multiedit tool reading sensitive credentials (GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47)
PraisonAI multiedit tool reading sensitive credentials (GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Python processes running PraisonAI (module 'praisonai.tools.multiedit') accessing files outside any reasonable workspace boundary — SSH private keys, AWS credentials, .env files, /etc/shadow. The multiedit tool's lack of path validation lets prompt-injected agents read arbitrary files via the dry_run diff output or direct read path. Rationale: Detection anchors on three article-specific tokens: (1) Python interpreter as initiating process, (2) 'praisonai' or 'multiedit' in command line (the vulnerable tool's module path is praisonai.tools.multiedit), (3) sensitive credential paths explicitly named in the article's Impact section (/etc/shadow, ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.aws/credentials, .env). The combination is high-fidelity because no legitimate workspace-scoped agent should be traversing to /etc/ or user home credential stores.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer explicitly asking PraisonAI agent to read or rotate their own ~/.aws/credentials in a personal lab environment
  • Legitimate PraisonAI workflow that ingests a project's .env file from inside the workspace (path will contain workspace root, not /root or $HOME)
  • Security researcher reproducing the GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47 PoC in a sandbox after the advisory landed
  • PraisonAI agent indexing a Git repository whose path happens to contain '.env.example' or similar template files
  • Automated dotfile sync tool spawned as a child of a PraisonAI orchestration session
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "/workspace/" or FolderPath has "/app/data/")
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "pytest" and FolderPath has "/tests/fixtures/")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the deployment shape — CLI dev workstation vs chatbot integration (Telegram/Discord/Slack with auto_approve_tools=True is the high-risk path). Pull the agent's prompt/conversation log around the file-access timestamp; the prompt that drove the multiedit call is the smoking gun. Step 2 (contain): If the file accessed was a credential store, immediately rotate the secret (SSH key, AWS access key, .env API keys) and revoke active sessions. Pin or remove the multiedit tool from the agent's tool registry until upgraded to praisonai >= 4.6.61. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same host for (a) outbound network connections from the Python process to non-corporate destinations in the 10 minutes following the read, (b) subsequent file WRITES by the same process to authorized_keys/.bashrc (see persistence UC), (c) other LLM agent tools in the org's stack with similar path-validation gaps.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
   or ActionType startswith "File"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe", "python3", "python", "python3.exe", "pythonw.exe", "python3.10", "python3.11", "python3.12")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "multiedit")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.ssh\", @"\.aws\", @"\.env", @"\.netrc", "/etc/shadow", "/etc/passwd", "/.ssh/", "/.aws/", "/root/", "id_rsa", "id_ed25519", "credentials")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python", "python3", "pythonw")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "multiedit")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.ssh/", "/.aws/", "/.env", "/.netrc", "/etc/shadow", "/etc/passwd", "id_rsa", "id_ed25519", "credentials", @"\.ssh\", @"\.aws\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PraisonAI MultiEdit Tool Accessing Sensitive Credentials
id: 8b3f4e2a-91c7-4a5d-b8f1-3e9c5d2a7f64
description: Detects the PraisonAI Python agent (vulnerable multiedit tool, GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47) reading credentials, SSH keys, or cloud secrets outside any plausible workspace. The multiedit tool lacks path validation and traversal protection.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.t1552.004
logsource:
  product: linux
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|contains: 'python'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'praisonai'
      - 'multiedit'
  selection_target:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/.ssh/id_'
      - '/.aws/credentials'
      - '/.aws/config'
      - '/.env'
      - '/.netrc'
      - '/etc/shadow'
      - '/etc/passwd'
      - 'authorized_keys'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_target
falsepositives:
  - Developer explicitly invoking PraisonAI to manage their own credentials/SSH keys
  - Automated PraisonAI workflows that legitimately read .env config from a known workspace
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:(PATH OR SYSCALL) @process.name:(python OR python3 OR pythonw) @process.command_line:(*praisonai* OR *multiedit*) @file.path:(*/.ssh/id_* OR */.aws/credentials* OR */.env OR */.netrc OR /etc/shadow OR /etc/passwd OR *authorized_keys*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| ContextImageFileName=/python[3]?(w)?(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("(/\.ssh/id_|/\.aws/credentials|/\.aws/config|/\.env$|/\.netrc|/etc/shadow|/etc/passwd|authorized_keys|\\\\\.ssh\\\\|\\\\\.aws\\\\)", field=TargetFileName)
| join({
    #event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
    | regex("(praisonai|multiedit)", field=CommandLine)
  }, field=ContextProcessId, key=TargetProcessId, include=[CommandLine, ImageFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
