PraisonAI multiedit writing to persistence locations (authorized_keys / shell rc / cron) AIInstallation High
Hunts the write-side abuse of the GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47 multiedit vulnerability — a Python PraisonAI process writing/modifying files in canonical Linux/Windows persistence locations (~/.ssh/authorized_keys, ~/.bashrc, ~/.bash_profile, ~/.profile, cron, autostart) where no workspace-scoped agent should ever touch. The advisory explicitly calls out writing to ~/.bashrc and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys as the privilege-escalation impact. Rationale: Anchors on the article's Impact section, which explicitly names ~/.bashrc and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys as the privilege-escalation outcomes. Combining the Python+praisonai/multiedit cmdline filter with these specific persistence paths makes this alerting-tier — there is essentially no legitimate scenario where a PraisonAI agent should rewrite a user's shell rc or SSH authorized_keys outside an explicit provisioning playbook.
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1546.004 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin using PraisonAI as a deliberate Ansible-style provisioner to push authorized_keys to fleet hosts
  • Developer asking PraisonAI to add an alias to their own .bashrc on a personal dev VM
  • Container/cloud-init bootstrap script that happens to embed PraisonAI for initial host config
  • Security researcher reproducing the PoC from the advisory
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "ansible" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "cloud-init")
| where not (DeviceName startswith "dev-" and AccountName == "developer")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Diff the modified file against backup/git history — the inserted content is the payload. Common shapes: a new SSH public key not matching any known engineer fingerprint, a curl|sh trampoline appended to .bashrc, an entry in cron.d calling out to an external URL. Pull the PraisonAI session/prompt that drove the write. Step 2 (contain): Revert the file from backup; if authorized_keys was modified, kill all live SSH sessions for that account and rotate any other access. Disable the agent integration (Telegram/Discord/Slack bot token, API key) and pin praisonai package to >= 4.6.61 across the fleet. Step 3 (hunt): Search 24h forward for SSH logins to this host from any IP whose pubkey matches the freshly-added one; search the org for other hosts where the same praisonai process wrote anywhere outside its workspace.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe", "python3", "python", "python3.exe", "pythonw.exe", "python3.10", "python3.11", "python3.12")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "multiedit")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.ssh/authorized_keys", "/.bashrc", "/.bash_profile", "/.profile", "/.zshrc", "/etc/cron.d", "/etc/crontab", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/sudoers", @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\")
   or FileName in~ ("authorized_keys", ".bashrc", ".bash_profile", ".profile", ".zshrc", "crontab", "sudoers")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          PreviousFileName, PreviousFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python", "python3", "pythonw")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "multiedit")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.ssh/authorized_keys", "/.bashrc", "/.bash_profile", "/.profile", "/.zshrc", "/etc/cron.d", "/etc/crontab", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/sudoers")
   or TargetFileName in~ ("authorized_keys", ".bashrc", ".bash_profile", ".profile", ".zshrc", "crontab", "sudoers")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable PraisonAI package exposure (< 4.6.61, GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47) AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces hosts running a vulnerable version of the pip:praisonai package so the SOC can drive remediation before exploitation. Pure exposure-management pivot — pairs with the credential-read and persistence detections above so any prior exploitation can be retrospectively hunted on confirmed-vulnerable hosts. Rationale: Targets the exact pip package + version range named in the advisory ('Affected packages: pip:praisonai (vuln < 4.6.61)'). This is the SOC's 'are we even exposed?' query — without it, the hunting detections above have no priority ordering for which hosts to investigate first.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped lab hosts where the vulnerable version is intentionally pinned for reproduction research
  • Hosts where Defender TVM has not yet inventoried pip packages (TVM coverage of Python packages is partial — absence does not mean clean)
  • Containers where the praisonai package lives inside an image that TVM cannot introspect
  • Pre-production hosts scheduled for teardown that won't be patched
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Prioritize the result set by IsInternetFacing == true and by chatbot deployment hosts (Telegram/Discord/Slack-integrated PraisonAI is the high-blast-radius shape per the advisory). Step 2 (contain): Drive upgrade to praisonai >= 4.6.61 via the org's pip/Poetry/uv channel; for hosts that can't upgrade immediately, set auto_approve_tools=False on any chatbot integration and remove multiedit from the agent's tool registry. Step 3 (hunt): For every host this query returns, retro-run the credential-read and persistence UCs over the last 90 days — if praisonai was vulnerable, any historical file-access to /etc/shadow or write to authorized_keys by that python process is high-priority IR work, not noise.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "praisonai" or SoftwareName == "praisonai"
| extend VersionParts = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(VersionParts[0]), Minor = toint(VersionParts[1]), Patch = toint(VersionParts[2])
| where Major < 4
   or (Major == 4 and Minor < 6)
   or (Major == 4 and Minor == 6 and Patch < 61)
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceInfo
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId
    | project DeviceId, IsInternetFacing, MachineGroup, LoggedOnUsers
  ) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion,
          OSPlatform, IsInternetFacing, MachineGroup, LoggedOnUsers
| order by tostring(IsInternetFacing) desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "praisonai"
| extend VersionParts = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")

Unauthenticated JSON-RPC tools/call hitting an internal MCP HTTP listener AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP POST traffic carrying JSON-RPC method strings ('tools/call','tools/list','resources/read','prompts/get') against the MCP server's default listener port. Targets the specific exploit shape from GHSA-j4f3-55x4-r6q2 where the praisonai TypeScript MCPServer accepts these methods with no Authorization check and binds to all interfaces. Rationale: Anchors on the article's two strongest fingerprints: (1) the specific JSON-RPC method strings handleRequest() dispatches without auth ('tools/call','tools/list','resources/read','prompts/get','initialize'), and (2) the default port 3000 + node.exe parent process running praisonai/mcp/server code. The Sentinel query also captures the article's PoV confirming 'Bearer invalid' is ignored — a Bearer-invalid POST that returns 200 is decisive.
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal MCP clients on the same host invoking tools/list against a development instance
  • Security scanners (Nuclei, Burp, internal pentest) probing JSON-RPC endpoints on port 3000
  • Loopback PoV/PoC runs by the developer hardening their MCP server
  • Other JSON-RPC services on port 3000 unrelated to praisonai (e.g. Ethereum-style RPC, internal dashboards)
  • Health-check / monitoring probes that send empty POST bodies
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("--test", "--scan", "NODE_ENV=development") | where RemoteIP !in (vuln_scanner_ips) | where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the offending host's praisonai version (`npm ls praisonai`) and confirm MCPServer.start() is called with HTTP transport; review the WAF/proxy log around the alert window for the source IP, JSON-RPC method, and whether Authorization header was present/valid. Step 2 (contain): if the listener is reachable from outside the trust boundary, block inbound 3000 at the host firewall, restart the node process bound to 127.0.0.1, or stop the service until a patched version (post-1.7.1 with auth wired) is deployed. Step 3 (hunt): for the same source IP, search EmailEvents and DeviceProcessEvents for follow-on activity — node.exe spawning cmd/powershell/bash (tool handler abuse), unexpected file writes by node.exe, and DNS/outbound from the node process to non-corp domains within 1 hour of the inbound JSON-RPC.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 3000
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "praisonai-ts", "mcp/server", "MCPServer")
| where RemoteIPType !in ("Loopback", "Private") or RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, LocalIP, LocalPort,
          InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 3000
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where Message has_any ('"method":"tools/call"', '"method":"tools/list"', '"method":"resources/read"', '"method":"prompts/get"', '"method":"initialize"')
| extend AuthHeaderPresent = Message has "Authorization:"
| extend AuthInvalid = Message has_cs "Authorization: Bearer invalid" or Message matches regex @"(?i)Authorization:\s*Bearer\s+(invalid|test|null|undefined)\b"
| where not(AuthHeaderPresent) or AuthInvalid
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, AuthHeaderPresent, AuthInvalid, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:3000 (@Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\NODE.EXE)) -CIDR(@SourceIp, 127.0.0.0/8) -CIDR(@SourceIp, ::1/128)

Vulnerable praisonai npm package (<=1.7.1) installed on host AIWeaponization High
Detects the on-disk fingerprint of the vulnerable npm package (`node_modules/praisonai/package.json` and the unguarded `src/praisonai-ts/src/mcp/server.ts` file) being written during `npm install`. Treat as a hunting hook to find every machine that needs patching before the wider attack-surface hunt. Rationale: Targets the exact file artefacts named in the article ('src/praisonai-ts/src/mcp/server.ts' and the npm package layout). Combining 'node_modules/praisonai' with an npm/yarn/pnpm parent eliminates source-checkout false positives. Pairs with UC1 — patch the hosts this lights up before UC1 trips for real.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer machines doing legitimate development against the praisonai source tree (not exposed to network)
  • CI build runners installing dependencies in ephemeral containers for testing
  • Security-research/sandbox VMs deliberately installing the vulnerable version for reproduction
  • Mirror/cache servers (Verdaccio, Artifactory) pre-fetching the package
  • Old development branches resurrected during git checkout that contain the package.json on disk but never serve it
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Users\\" | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\" | where DeviceName !in (dev_workstations_watchlist)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): for each host, capture `node_modules/praisonai/package.json` `version` and `dependencies`; confirm whether the host runs `MCPServer.start({port:...})` in production code (grep repo for `MCPServer` instantiation). Step 2 (contain): if production, force-upgrade to a patched version once published or pin to a fork that wires MCPSecurity into startHttp() and binds to 127.0.0.1; in the interim, add a host-firewall rule blocking inbound 3000 from non-loopback. Step 3 (hunt): for every host that has the file, pivot to UC1 over the last 30 days to check whether anyone has already exploited it; pull `node.exe` outbound DNS and process-tree for the same window.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has "node_modules\\praisonai" or FolderPath has "node_modules/praisonai" or FolderPath has "praisonai-ts\\src\\mcp" or FolderPath has "praisonai-ts/src/mcp"
| where FileName in~ ("package.json", "server.ts", "server.js")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe", "npm-cli.js", "node.exe", "pnpm.exe", "yarn.exe", "corepack.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,

| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where EventType =~ "FileCreated" or EventType =~ "FileRenamed"
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules/praisonai" or TargetFilePath has "node_modules\\praisonai" or TargetFilePath has "praisonai-ts/src/mcp" or TargetFilePath has "praisonai-ts\\src\\mcp"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("package.json", "server.ts", "server.js")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm", "node", "pnpm", "yarn", "corepack")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js praisonai MCP server spawning shell or scripting interpreter (tool-call abuse) AIActions on Objectives High
Post-exploitation pivot: an unauthenticated tools/call from UC1 lets the attacker invoke whatever tool handlers the MCPServer registered. Many handlers wrap shell, file, or db actions. This catches node.exe (with praisonai in its cmdline) spawning cmd/powershell/bash/sh as a child — the most common abuse shape regardless of which specific tool is registered. Rationale: The article notes 'MCP tools commonly wrap filesystem operations, API clients, database queries, agent actions, deployment operations, email/Slack actions, browser automation, and code execution'. A node.exe parent whose cmdline references praisonai/MCPServer spawning a shell or scripting interpreter is the single highest-fidelity post-exploit signature regardless of which tool was registered, and pairs cleanly with UC1 as the network-side trigger.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1059.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate registered MCP tools that genuinely wrap shell commands (e.g. a 'run_terminal' tool) used by the application's own AI agent loop
  • Developer testing the MCPServer locally with example tools that exec shell
  • npm postinstall scripts running during package upgrade (node spawning shell briefly)
  • CI/CD pipelines using praisonai for build-step orchestration that legitimately spawn shells
  • Application healthcheck/monitoring scripts invoked by node parent
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !has_any ("npm install", "npm run", "node-gyp", "yarn install") | where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("npm.exe", "yarn.exe", "pnpm.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): grab the child process commandline, hash, and any spawned descendants — confirm whether the action looks like a registered MCP tool's legitimate work or arbitrary attacker input (recon strings, encoded payloads, outbound network from the child). Pull the inbound JSON-RPC request from UC1 in the same minute. Step 2 (contain): isolate the host (or stop the node MCP service), revoke any credentials accessible to the node process (env vars, IAM role, .aws/credentials, .npmrc tokens). Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the child's outbound DNS/IPs and any file writes for next-stage payloads; check the source IP of the UC1 request against threat intel and enumerate every other host running praisonai (UC2) for the same source-IP probes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "praisonai-ts", "MCPServer", "mcp/server", "mcp\\server")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "bash.exe", "wsl.exe", "sh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "curl.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "praisonai-ts", "MCPServer", "mcp/server", "mcp\\server")

node.exe spawn loading vulnerable PraisonAI AgentOS package (npm:praisonai 1.6.0-1.7.1) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for Node.js processes executing the published praisonai npm package's AgentOS HTTP server. Per GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f, versions 1.6.0-1.7.1 ship dist/os/agentos.js that binds 0.0.0.0 without auth — finding these processes lets the SOC inventory exposed installations and confirm whether host is mitigated. Rationale: Uses the exact source path component 'dist/os/agentos' and module name 'praisonai' named in the advisory at src/praisonai-ts/src/os/agentos.ts. node.exe + these strings together is extremely high-fidelity because only deployments of this specific package match. Cross-checked the npm registry tarball naming convention. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal developers running praisonai for sanctioned LLM workflows
  • CI pipelines testing the praisonai package
  • Security team running the PoV reproduction to validate the advisory
  • Software inventory scanners that enumerate node_modules paths via cmdline
  • Developer running 'npm test' or 'npm run dev' on a praisonai fork during patch development
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("npm.exe", "npm-cli.js", "jest.exe") | where ProcessCommandLine !has "--test" and ProcessCommandLine !has "pov_poc"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the npm package version with 'npm ls praisonai' on the host or read package.json — only 1.6.0-1.7.1 are vulnerable; <=1.5.4 did not ship dist/os/agentos.js. Identify whether the listener bound 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1 via netstat / Get-NetTCPConnection on the AgentOS port. Step 2 (contain): If the server is internet-reachable or on a multi-tenant network, kill the node.exe process and block inbound on the AgentOS port at host firewall. Engage the application owner to rebind to 127.0.0.1 or add a reverse proxy with auth. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to the next UC (unauth /api/agents and /api/chat requests) over the last 30 days against the host's IPs to determine whether the exposure was already exploited; review agent.chat tool definitions to map blast radius (file/exec/MCP/business tools).

| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthenticated requests to PraisonAI AgentOS /api/agents or /api/chat endpoints AIExploitation High
Hunts proxy/WAF/IIS logs and EDR network telemetry for HTTP requests to the two exposed AgentOS routes named in the advisory. Because the vulnerable server registers /api/agents and /api/chat with no auth middleware between body parsing and route registration, any inbound hit to these paths from a non-loopback source on a host running praisonai 1.6.0-1.7.1 is likely exploitation. Rationale: Pivots on the exact route paths /api/agents and /api/chat named at agentos.ts lines 235 and 250 in the advisory, combined with the default port 8000 from app.serve({ port: 8000 }) and node.exe parent. The advisory's PoV control proves these paths return 200 without an Authorization header — checking for absent Authorization header in proxy logs converts the route-pattern signal into near-zero-FP detection. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

  • Internal authorized callers of AgentOS where the team built their own client without Authorization header (pre-patch architecture)
  • Health-check or uptime monitoring probes hitting /api/agents (e.g. Datadog Synthetics, Pingdom)
  • PraisonAI's own integration tests run against a staging deployment
  • Internal red-team or vuln-scanner activity (Nuclei, Burp) validating the GHSA
  • Developer curl from a non-loopback workstation during local debugging of a dev AgentOS instance

| where SourceIP !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1") | where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Pingdom", "DatadogSynthetics", "UptimeRobot", "StatusCake")

Step 1 (triage): Confirm the destination host is running praisonai 1.6.0-1.7.1 (see UC1). Pull full request bodies — POST /api/chat carries the attacker's prompt in the 'message' field; GET /api/agents leaks agent names/roles/first 100 chars of instructions. Identify the agent_name in the response to scope blast radius. Step 2 (contain): Block source IP at the perimeter; if exploitation appears successful (200 status from /api/chat with a non-empty response), rotate any credentials in the AgentOS process environment and revoke tool-side secrets the configured agent could reach (MCP tokens, API keys, DB creds). Take the AgentOS process offline pending patch — no fixed npm version exists, so apply the advisory's suggested bearer-token middleware patch or rebind to 127.0.0.1. Step 3 (hunt): Query for the same source IPs hitting any agent-named endpoints across the fleet, search egress logs for outbound traffic from node.exe to attacker-controlled infrastructure post-exploitation, and revi

Node.js spawning shell with reconnaissance commands (PraisonAI codeMode sandbox escape) AIExploitation High
Detects node/node.exe spawning sh/bash/cmd/powershell that immediately runs reconnaissance commands (whoami, uname, /etc/passwd, ~/.ssh). This is the post-RCE primitive demonstrated in the GHSA-p69m-4f92-2v84 PoC where `cp.execSync('id')` was used to confirm sandbox escape via `Function('return this')()` + `global.require('child_'+'process')`. Catches exploitation of any JS sandbox-escape pattern that ends in child_process invocation, not just PraisonAI. Rationale: The GHSA's PoC explicitly demonstrates RCE via `cp.execSync('id').toString()` after escaping the sandbox with `Function('return this')()` and `global.require('child_'+'process')`. Whatever the attacker prompt-injects into `codeMode`, the deterministic OS-level signal is the same: node spawns a shell (Node child_process always exec's via /bin/sh or cmd.exe), and the spawned shell runs recon. Pairing parent=node with child=shell with a recon-command cmdline gives high fidelity because legitimate Node apps rarely shell out to enumerate /etc/passwd or ~/.ssh. I did not web-search — this is a fresh advisory (published <30 days) with no expected secondary corroboration yet.
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.003 T1082 T1033 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node-based CI/CD agents (Jenkins agents, GitHub Actions runners, GitLab runners written in Node) executing pipeline scripts that call hostname/whoami for build metadata
  • Node.js diagnostic / health-check libraries (e.g. systeminformation, node-os-utils) shelling out to ifconfig or uname for system info
  • Containerized Node services running an entrypoint script that prints hostname/whoami at startup for logging
  • npm postinstall scripts that probe the environment (e.g. node-gyp builds detecting kernel version with uname -r)
  • Developer-machine Node REPL sessions where engineers manually run cp.execSync('whoami') for testing
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp", "node-pre-gyp", "systeminformation", "node-os-utils", "/actions-runner/", "/gitlab-runner/", "/jenkins/") or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"^(?:/bin/sh|/bin/bash)\s+-c\s+\"?hostname\"?\s*$")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the parent Node command line (InitiatingProcessCommandLine) and the script that was being executed. Look for `praisonai`, `codeMode`, `new Function(`, `with (sandbox)`, or `Function('return this')` in process args, loaded scripts, or recent npm package.json on the host. Check the spawning Node process's exposure — is it an LLM-agent backend reachable from the internet? Step 2 — Contain: if praisonai-ts <=1.7.1 is installed and the Node process is internet-exposed, stop the service, snapshot the host, and rotate any credentials in the process environment (env-var API keys are the GHSA's stated impact). Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId for (a) DeviceFileEvents to /tmp, /var/tmp, ~/.ssh, or .bashrc by node; (b) DeviceNetworkEvents from the node ProcessId to public IPs (exfil/C2); (c) DeviceProcessEvents for follow-on curl/wget/bash -i invocations spawned in the same logon session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(whoami|uname|hostname|ifconfig)\b"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd", "/etc/shadow", "~/.ssh", "/root/.ssh", "ip addr", "cat /root/", "id;", "id |", "id&&")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "code-mode", "codeMode", "new Function", "Function('return this')") 
   or AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, ProcessId, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\node.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "/node"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/sh" or NewProcessName endswith "/bash" or NewProcessName endswith "/dash" or NewProcessName endswith "/zsh"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(whoami|uname|hostname|ifconfig)\b"
   or CommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd", "/etc/shadow", "~/.ssh", "/root/.ssh", "ip addr", "cat /root/")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, NewProcessId, ProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects node/node.exe spawning a shell that runs reconnaissance commands. High-fidelity post-RCE signal for JavaScript sandbox-escape vulnerabilities such as PraisonAI codeMode (GHSA-p69m-4f92-2v84) where attacker-controlled code reaches child_process via the global object.

(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe) @CommandLine:(*whoami* OR *uname* OR */etc/passwd* OR */etc/shadow* OR *hostname* OR *ifconfig* OR *\"ip addr\"* OR *~/.ssh*)) OR (source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.parent.name:node @process.command_line:(*whoami* OR *uname* OR */etc/passwd* OR */etc/shadow* OR *hostname* OR *ifconfig* OR *\"ip addr\"* OR *~/.ssh* OR */root/.ssh*))

Vulnerable PraisonAI-TS package (<=1.7.1) installed — GHSA-p69m-4f92-2v84 AIWeaponization High
Hunts for hosts with the npm package `praisonai` (or `praisonai-ts`) at a version <=1.7.1 installed, which is vulnerable to the codeMode tool sandbox-escape RCE. Catches at-risk inventory before exploitation. Pivots on TVM software inventory and on file-event evidence of the package directory. Rationale: The GHSA names the exact vulnerable package and ceiling (`praisonai <=1.7.1`) and the exact file path (`src/praisonai-ts/src/tools/builtins/code-mode.ts`). DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory gives clean inventory for hosts where the package is registered; the DeviceFileEvents fallback catches hand-installed copies or container-baked images that TVM may not enumerate. Sentinel KQL is empty because the analyst-tenant Sentinel schema in this environment does not expose DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory or a file-event table covering node_modules paths — operators should hunt this via Defender XDR or the npm-audit pipeline. CloudWatch is empty for the same reason (not AWS telemetry).
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Inventory.Software
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal security-research/test hosts deliberately running the vulnerable version to validate detections — keep but tag
  • Developer workstations with the package in a sandboxed test directory unrelated to production services
  • Container build hosts where the image is built but never executed in production (pre-bake CI runners)
  • Vendored copies inside another repo (node_modules of a different project that depends on praisonai transitively but isn't internet-exposed)
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sec-research-", "detection-lab-", "-buildagent-") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("docker.exe", "containerd-shim.exe", "buildkitd"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: for each hit, determine whether the host is internet-exposed and whether the praisonai agent is actually instantiated with `codeMode` enabled (grep the host's app config for `code-mode`, `codeMode`, or `tools: [codeMode]`). If codeMode is not enabled, downgrade to advisory; the vulnerable code path requires the tool to be wired into an agent. Step 2 — Contain: for exposed services with codeMode enabled, force-pin the dependency to a patched version (>=1.7.2 once published) or disable the codeMode tool in agent config; rotate any API keys/secrets present in the Node process environment. Step 3 — Hunt: cross-reference hit hosts against UC #1 (Node spawning shell with recon) over the past 30d to confirm no prior exploitation. Add the package directory to a watch-list for change events (new versions, new installs) until the org-wide upgrade is complete.
// Inventory pass — vulnerable versions per Defender TVM
let vuln = DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
  | where SoftwareName has "praisonai"
  | where SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^(0\.|1\.[0-6]\.|1\.7\.[01](?:$|[^0-9]))"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion;
// Filesystem fallback — catches manual / non-managed installs TVM missed
let fileEvidence = DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)node_modules[\\/]praisonai(?:-ts)?[\\/]"
  | where FileName =~ "package.json"
  | summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Paths=make_set(FolderPath, 25) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName;
union isfuzzy=true vuln, fileEvidence
| order by DeviceName asc
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\node_modules\\praisonai\\package.json OR *\\node_modules\\praisonai-ts\\package.json)) OR (source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:PATH @name:(*\/node_modules\/praisonai\/package.json OR *\/node_modules\/praisonai-ts\/package.json))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/node_modules[\\\/]praisonai(?:-ts)?[\\\/]package\.json$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Installation of vulnerable npm praisonai package (GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp) AIInstallation High
Detects npm, yarn or pnpm installing the 'praisonai' package. Versions through 1.7.1 ship a built-in 'codeMode' tool whose advertised sandbox can be escaped via the JavaScript Function-constructor prototype chain — this surfaces hosts that will harbour the vulnerable agent-tool surface until patched. Rationale: Pivots on the exact package name 'praisonai' from the advisory plus the standard npm/yarn/pnpm/node install verbs. The advisory explicitly names version 1.7.1 as PoV-confirmed and the package as a published npm artifact, so install activity is the definitive supply-chain pivot.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application developer installing PraisonAI for legitimate agent-framework evaluation
  • CI/CD pipeline pinning a project dependency that already includes praisonai
  • Container build step installing dependencies on a build-host
  • Security researcher reproducing the advisory PoV in a lab

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chocolatey.exe","choco.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "jenkins" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "gitlab-runner"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the npm version installed by inspecting node_modules/praisonai/package.json; flag any version <= 1.7.1 (post-disclosure cut-off until upstream patch). Identify whether the host is dev, CI, or production-facing. 2) Contain: for production hosts, isolate or stop the Node.js service that loads praisonai until upgrade. For CI, pin to a patched version (or remove the codeMode tool). 3) Hunt: across the org, list every host with package praisonai installed via software inventory (DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory) and look for any node.exe children spawning cmd/powershell/sh in the prior 30 days — see related UC for the escape pattern.

PraisonAI codeMode Function-constructor sandbox escape payload AIExploitation High
Hunts for the literal JavaScript prototype-chain escape string that bypasses the codeMode blocklist — ({}).constructor.constructor('return process')() and process.mainModule.require — appearing in Node.js command lines, script files, or agent prompt logs. This is the exact payload the advisory's PoV uses to escape the advertised sandbox. Rationale: These exact strings appear in the advisory's Technical Details section — ({}).constructor.constructor('return process')() is the prototype-chain escape, process.mainModule.require is the post-escape pivot to fs/child_process, and 'with (sandbox)' is the literal wrapper the codeMode implementation uses. Any of these in process telemetry or script content is a high-fidelity exploit signal.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1480 T1211
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or detection engineer testing this very rule with the PoV
  • Static linter / SAST tool scanning JavaScript supply chain for prototype-chain abuse patterns
  • CTF challenge or training material demonstrating Function-constructor escapes
  • Application that legitimately uses 'with (sandbox)' for some non-security DSL — rare in modern JS
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\node_modules\\eslint\\","\\node_modules\\sonarqube\\","semgrep","codeql") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("eslint","semgrep","codeql","sonar"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source — was the string in a Node.js command line (node -e), a written .js file under a praisonai project, or an agent prompt log? Pull the surrounding process tree (parent of node.exe + any spawned children) for the same aid in a 10-minute window. 2) Contain: kill the offending node.exe / pwsh / cmd lineage, isolate the host from network, snapshot for forensics. Rotate any secrets readable from process env (the advisory PoV reads host environment variables first). 3) Hunt: across the org, search the same patterns in EmailEvents subjects (LLM agents over chat), UrlClickEvents Url, and persistent script directories. Pull all hosts with praisonai installed (DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory) and review their last 30 days of node.exe child-process spawns.
let escape_patterns = dynamic(["constructor.constructor","process.mainModule.require","return process","with (sandbox)"]);
(union isfuzzy=true
    (DeviceProcessEvents
     | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
     | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (escape_patterns)
        or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (escape_patterns)
     | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source="Process", FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
    (DeviceFileEvents
     | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
     | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
     | where FileName endswith ".js" or FileName endswith ".ts" or FileName endswith ".mjs" or FileName endswith ".cjs" or FileName endswith ".json"
     | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe")
     | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (escape_patterns)
        or FolderPath has "praisonai"
     | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="File", FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
)
| order by Timestamp desc
let escape_patterns = dynamic(["constructor.constructor","process.mainModule.require","return process","with (sandbox)"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any (escape_patterns)
   or ParentProcessName has_any (escape_patterns)
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\node.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\sh","\\bash")
   or ParentProcessName has "node.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

node.exe spawning shell or LOLBin child — post-codeMode-escape execution AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the post-escape signal: after the sandbox bypass, the attacker reaches process.mainModule.require('child_process') and spawns a host shell. Detects node.exe parenting cmd.exe, powershell.exe, sh, bash, wmic, certutil and similar LOLBins — uncommon in normal Node.js service workloads. Rationale: The advisory PoV explicitly demonstrates the escape ending in process.mainModule.require('child_process') with a 'harmless printf' — meaning node.exe spawns a host shell. node.exe rarely parents cmd/powershell/sh/bash in normal server workloads, so this child-list pivoted on a node.exe parent is a precise post-exploit signal regardless of which Node.js sandbox library was bypassed.
ATT&CKT1059 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Electron desktop applications invoking shell helpers (e.g. VSCode terminal, Slack)
  • Build tooling such as Webpack/Vite/Next.js running git or npm subprocesses on dev workstations
  • Headless test frameworks (Playwright, Puppeteer) shelling out for browser launches
  • Legitimate Node.js admin scripts that call out to certutil for cert installation
  • CI runners on build agents — narrow to production-tier hosts to drop these
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\Electron\\","\\Code\\","\\Slack\\","\\Discord\\","\\Teams\\","\\VSCode\\")) and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("webpack","vite","next dev","playwright","puppeteer","jest"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the offending node.exe — parent (was it the praisonai agent service?), siblings, and child cmd-line. Check the InitiatingProcessCommandLine of node.exe for 'praisonai' references and dump the loaded module list if possible. 2) Contain: kill the node.exe lineage and isolate the host. Revoke API tokens and rotate secrets held in the host's environment (advisory shows env-var read is the first post-escape action). 3) Hunt: across the org, identify every host running a Node service that depends on praisonai (DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory + dependency manifests). Review last 30 days of any node.exe parent → shell child, prioritising those with internet egress immediately after.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wmic.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","sh","bash","dash","zsh","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","reg.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend PraisonAILoaded = iff(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "praisonai", "yes", "unknown")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, PraisonAILoaded, SHA256
| order by PraisonAILoaded desc, Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wmic.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\net.exe","\\reg.exe","/bin/sh","/bin/bash","/usr/bin/bash")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend PraisonAILoaded = iff(ParentProcessName has "praisonai" or CommandLine has "praisonai", "yes", "unknown")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, PraisonAILoaded

PraisonAI codeMode blocklist trigger — sandbox probing in application logs AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for the literal 'Blocked pattern detected:' error string that codeMode emits to stderr when its regex blocklist catches require('fs') / require('child_process') / process.exit / eval. Multiple blocks from a single host/user is high-confidence evidence of an attacker probing the sandbox before pivoting to the prototype-chain escape. Rationale: The advisory's PoV output literally shows 'Blocked pattern detected: require\\s*\\(\\s*['\"]fs['\"]\\s*\\)' and 'Code contains blocked patterns for security' as the codeMode stderr when its blocklist fires. These exact strings appearing in stderr/file logs — especially repeated from one host or one agent session — are evidence of an attacker enumerating the blocklist before pivoting to the Function-constructor escape.
ATT&CKT1480 T1059.007 T1212
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer locally testing codeMode tool with naive payloads while building an agent
  • Security researcher reproducing the advisory PoV
  • Unit tests for the praisonai package validating the blocklist works
  • One-off LLM hallucination where the model tried require('fs') and got blocked once
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("dev-","-dev","build-","ci-","runner-")) and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm test","jest","mocha","vitest"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the surrounding context — what code did the agent try to run? Identify the calling user / session ID / prompt that led to the block. Single blocks may be benign; repeated blocks from the same session are the IOC. 2) Contain: if the same session subsequently emits constructor.constructor or process.mainModule.require strings (cross-reference UC2), treat as confirmed escape — isolate the Node host, rotate any secrets in env, kill the agent session. 3) Hunt: review last 30 days of the same agent service for blocked-pattern occurrences and join with subsequent process spawns from node.exe (UC3) within a 5-minute window per session — the chain block→escape→child_process is the highest-confidence sequence.
let blocklist_strings = dynamic(["Blocked pattern detected:","Code contains blocked patterns for security","require\\s*\\(\\s*['\"]fs['\"]","require\\s*\\(\\s*['\"]child_process['\"]"]);
(union isfuzzy=true
    (DeviceProcessEvents
     | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
     | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (blocklist_strings) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (blocklist_strings)
     | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source="Process", FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName),
    (DeviceFileEvents
     | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
     | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
     | where FolderPath has_any ("praisonai","\\logs\\","\\log\\","stderr")
     | where FileName endswith ".log" or FileName endswith ".err" or FileName endswith ".txt" or FileName endswith ".json"
     | summarize WriteCount=count(), Files=make_set(FileName, 25) by bin(Timestamp, 1h), DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath
     | where WriteCount >= 3)
)
| order by Timestamp desc
let blocklist_strings = dynamic(["Blocked pattern detected:","Code contains blocked patterns for security"]);

| summarize BlockCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Samples = make_set(SyslogMessage, 5) by HostName, ProcessName
| where BlockCount >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Salesforce REST API /sobjects schema enumeration burst per principal
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Klue Battlecards connected-app activity from Icarus IPs in Salesforce
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network egress to Icarus extortion C2 IPs (Klue OAuth campaign) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Salesforce REST API /query burst — >500 calls in 15-minute window · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Network egress to Icarus extortion C2 IPs (Klue OAuth campaign) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any outbound or inbound traffic to the four IPs ReliaQuest and Huntress published as Icarus infrastructure driving Salesforce REST API exfiltration during the Klue Battlecards OAuth breach. Catches both endpoint-side beacons and CASB/proxy-logged SaaS connections sourced from those IPs. Rationale: Both ReliaQuest and Huntress publish the same four IPs as Icarus infrastructure, satisfying the two-source corroboration bar. Anchored on the verbatim IOC block from the article. The union shape lets one rule cover endpoint egress, CASB/proxy, and AAD sign-ins, which is important because the Klue attacker pivots primarily land on SaaS log surfaces rather than EDR. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft • https://www.huntress.com/blog/klue-breach-investigation • https://www.govinfosecurity.com/attackers-steal-salesforce-data-from-klue-battlecards-users-a-32011
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel platform reaching out to verify the published IPs
  • Researcher/red-team box egressing through the same hosting provider as Icarus
  • IP re-allocation by the hosting provider weeks after the campaign
  • Tor/VPN exit-node coincidence if any IP is reused as a public proxy
  • Salesforce/Klue trust-ops investigation traffic during the disclosed incident window
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify which IP fired and which user/service principal/integration owned the session. If the Salesforce Klue Battlecards connected app is the carrier, jump immediately to UC4 to confirm whether bulk REST API queries followed. 2. Contain: revoke OAuth refresh tokens for the Klue Battlecards connected app in Salesforce Setup → Connected Apps → Manage, terminate active sessions for the impacted user, and block the four IPs at the perimeter and via a Conditional Access named-location deny. 3. Hunt: pivot Salesforce REST API logs in the same hour for /services/data/v*/sobjects and /services/data/v*/query traffic from any IP, and pull Klue Battlecards activity for the prior 30 days to scope token use.
let IcarusIPs = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteIP in (IcarusIPs)
  | project Timestamp, Source="Endpoint", DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine ),
( CloudAppEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where IPAddress in (IcarusIPs)
  | project Timestamp, Source="SaaS", DeviceName=ObjectName, AccountName=AccountDisplayName, RemoteIP=IPAddress, RemotePort=int(null), InitiatingProcessFileName=Application, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=tostring(RawEventData) ),
( AADSignInEventsBeta
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where IPAddress in (IcarusIPs)
  | project Timestamp, Source="AAD", DeviceName=DeviceName, AccountName=AccountUpn, RemoteIP=IPAddress, RemotePort=int(null), InitiatingProcessFileName=Application, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=UserAgent )
| order by Timestamp desc
let IcarusIPs = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where SourceIP in (IcarusIPs) or DestinationIP in (IcarusIPs)
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="CEF", DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, SourceUserName ),
( SigninLogs
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where IPAddress in (IcarusIPs)
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="AAD", UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, ResultDescription ),
( ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where SrcIpAddr in (IcarusIPs) or DstIpAddr in (IcarusIPs)
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="ASIM", DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Klue Battlecards connected-app activity from Icarus IPs in Salesforce AIDelivery Medium
Hunts CloudAppEvents Salesforce telemetry for activity attributable to the Klue Battlecards connected app sourced from the four published Icarus IPs. This is the smoking-gun pivot: the campaign hinges on stolen Klue Battlecards OAuth tokens being replayed against customer Salesforce orgs from those IPs. Rationale: Pairs the two highest-fidelity pivots the article names: the Klue Battlecards connected app (Salesforce publicly stated they disabled this integration) and the four ReliaQuest/Huntress IPs. CloudAppEvents is the right surface because Defender for Cloud Apps' Salesforce connector preserves connected-app attribution. Sentinel/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty because Salesforce REST API activity does not land in a canonical table on those platforms by default — wire via MCAS→Sentinel CloudAppEvents passthrough or the Salesforce_CL connector and re-target as needed. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft • https://www.huntress.com/blog/klue-breach-investigation • https://status.salesforce.com/generalmessages/20000257
ATT&CKT1199 T1078.004 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Klue NOC remediation traffic during the disclosed incident window if their egress overlaps the published ranges
  • Customer-side legitimate Klue Battlecards sync on the same day pre-token-revocation
  • Salesforce trust-ops investigation actions on the connected app
  • Manual admin re-test of the integration during incident response
Suppression filter
| where not (tostring(RawEventData) has "salesforce.com/trust" and ISP has_any ("Salesforce","Heroku"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify Salesforce user(s) tied to AccountDisplayName and the impacted Salesforce org; pull Connected Apps OAuth Usage for the 14 days prior to find token issuance time. 2. Contain: revoke the Klue Battlecards connected-app OAuth refresh tokens for the impacted org, terminate active Salesforce sessions, treat queried SObjects as potentially exposed. 3. Hunt: run UC3 (sobjects schema enumeration) and UC4 (bulk query burst) against the same time window to determine whether exfil completed or was caught mid-recon; check AADSignInEventsBeta for service-principal token redemption from the same IPs.
let IcarusIPs = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);

   or ConnectedApp has "Klue Battlecards"

Salesforce REST API /sobjects schema enumeration burst per principal AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the Icarus reconnaissance pattern ReliaQuest described: an actor walks /services/data/v59.0/sobjects to fingerprint every SObject in the org before deciding what to steal. Distinct object-path counts from a single principal/hour rise far above what legitimate integrations need. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim '/services/data/v59.0/sobjects' endpoint that ReliaQuest specifically called out as the recon step. Distinct-object fan-out per principal is the high-fidelity tell because Klue Battlecards and other legitimate connected apps query a known fixed object set (Account, Opportunity, Contact, custom battlecard objects) — not the entire SObject catalog. Threshold of 30 is conservative; tune per tenant baseline. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft
ATT&CKT1526 T1087.004
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Salesforce admin running Workbench or Schema Builder for a metadata audit
  • New ETL connector first-time enumeration during onboarding
  • Developer running sfdx force:schema:sobject:list against a sandbox
  • Backup tool (OwnBackup, Spanning, Odaseva) initial seed run touching every object
  • DevOps tool (Gearset, Copado) doing a metadata diff pre-deploy
Suppression filter
| where SampleConnectedApps !has_any ("OwnBackup","Spanning Backup","Odaseva","Workbench","Salesforce Inspector","Gearset","Copado","Fivetran","Stitch")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the AccountDisplayName and ConnectedApp — Workbench appears as 'Salesforce Workbench' or a named user, integrations appear as their connected-app name. If neither known-admin nor allow-listed integration, escalate. 2. Contain: revoke the user's active Salesforce sessions and the connected app's OAuth tokens; require step-up MFA for re-auth. 3. Hunt: pivot forward 0–24h on same user/IP into UC4 (bulk /query burst) to determine whether enumeration converted to exfiltration; cross-check SampleIPs against UC1 (Icarus IOC list).
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| extend Uri = tostring(RawEventData.URI), ConnectedApp = tostring(RawEventData.ApplicationName)
| where Uri matches regex @"/services/data/v\d+\.\d+/sobjects"
| summarize DistinctObjectPaths = dcount(Uri),
            TotalHits = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleConnectedApps = make_set(ConnectedApp, 10),
            SampleIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            SampleUris = make_set(Uri, 25)
            by bin(Timestamp, 1h), AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId
| where DistinctObjectPaths > 30   // legit integrations hit a small fixed set; Icarus walks the catalog
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| extend Uri = tostring(RawEventData.URI), ConnectedApp = tostring(RawEventData.ApplicationName)
| where Uri matches regex @"/services/data/v\d+\.\d+/sobjects"
| summarize DistinctObjectPaths = dcount(Uri),
            TotalHits = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleConnectedApps = make_set(ConnectedApp, 10),
            SampleIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            SampleUris = make_set(Uri, 25)
            by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h), AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId
| where DistinctObjectPaths > 30   // legit integrations hit a small fixed set; Icarus walks the catalog
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
`cim_Web_indexes` sourcetype=salesforce* uri_path="*/services/data/v*/sobjects*" | bucket _time span=1h | stats dc(uri_path) as DistinctObjectPaths count as TotalHits values(connected_app) as ConnectedApps values(src_ip) as SrcIPs by _time user | where DistinctObjectPaths > 30 | sort - _time
Salesforce REST API /query burst — >500 calls in 15-minute window AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on the exfiltration shape ReliaQuest documented: after slow steady reconnaissance, the Icarus actor sent nearly 1,000 /services/data/v59.0/query calls in a 15-minute window. Bursts of this magnitude per principal/connected-app fall well outside any Klue or legitimate ETL sync cadence and are diagnostic of automated CRM scraping. Rationale: Threshold is grounded in the ReliaQuest quote of '~1000 queries in a 15-minute window'; 500 is a safe trip-point that still captures the Icarus burst shape while leaving headroom for one-off legitimate backfills. BurstSeconds helps the analyst distinguish the slow steady recon pull (first stage) from the rapid exfiltration burst (second stage). Sentinel/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: Salesforce REST API telemetry does not land in canonical tables on those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft • https://www.huntress.com/blog/klue-breach-investigation
ATT&CKT1530 T1567 T1119
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Marketing cloud (Marketo / Pardot / HubSpot) one-off backfill
  • Data-warehouse ETL pull (Fivetran / Stitch / Snowflake) first run or post-schema-change resync
  • Custom reporting job kicked off by sales-ops engineer
  • Salesforce sandbox refresh replaying through a CI integration test
  • Backup tool (OwnBackup, Spanning) full-org snapshot
Suppression filter
| where ConnectedApps !has_any ("Fivetran","Stitch","OwnBackup","Spanning Backup","Odaseva","Marketo","HubSpot Sync","Pardot","Snowflake")
| where AccountDisplayName !endswith "@etl-svc.yourdomain.com"
Response runbook
1. Triage: pivot on AccountDisplayName + ConnectedApp + SrcIPs from the alert; cross-check SrcIPs against UC1 (Icarus IOC list). If ConnectedApp is 'Klue Battlecards' OR SrcIPs intersect the Icarus list, escalate to incident and treat the queried SObjects as exfiltrated. 2. Contain: revoke the connected-app OAuth refresh tokens for the impacted user(s) and terminate active sessions; if Klue Battlecards, confirm Salesforce's tenant-wide disablement is in place. 3. Hunt: replay the /query URIs via Salesforce Event Monitoring to reconstruct exact SOQL and the SObjects/records returned, then notify legal/privacy for downstream breach-notification scoping; check for matching outbound POST traffic from any internal Klue connector host to the Icarus IPs.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| extend Uri = tostring(RawEventData.URI), ConnectedApp = tostring(RawEventData.ApplicationName)
| where Uri matches regex @"/services/data/v\d+\.\d+/query"
| summarize QueryCount = count(),
            DistinctQueries = dcount(Uri),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            BurstSeconds = datetime_diff('second', max(Timestamp), min(Timestamp)),
            SrcIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            ConnectedApps = make_set(ConnectedApp, 5)
            by bin(Timestamp, 15m), AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId
| where QueryCount > 500   // ReliaQuest observed ~1000 queries in a 15-min window from Icarus
| order by QueryCount desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| extend Uri = tostring(RawEventData.URI), ConnectedApp = tostring(RawEventData.ApplicationName)
| where Uri matches regex @"/services/data/v\d+\.\d+/query"
| summarize QueryCount = count(),
            DistinctQueries = dcount(Uri),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            BurstSeconds = datetime_diff('second', max(TimeGenerated), min(TimeGenerated)),
            SrcIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            ConnectedApps = make_set(ConnectedApp, 5)
            by bin(TimeGenerated, 15m), AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId
| where QueryCount > 500   // ReliaQuest observed ~1000 queries in a 15-min window from Icarus
| order by QueryCount desc
WEB
`cim_Web_indexes` sourcetype=salesforce* uri_path="*/services/data/v*/query*" | bucket _time span=15m | stats count as QueryCount dc(uri_path) as DistinctQueries values(connected_app) as ConnectedApp values(src_ip) as SrcIPs by _time user | where QueryCount > 500 | sort - QueryCount
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason

INC ransomware BYOVD vulnerable filter-driver load (filwfp.sys / filnk.sys / fildds.sys) AIInstallation High
Detects load or install of the three vulnerable filter-system drivers (filwfp.sys, filnk.sys, fildds.sys) that INC ransomware affiliates abuse via BYOVD to impair Defender/EDR before encryption. These driver names are highly article-specific and not common in legitimate enterprise software. Rationale: filwfp.sys, filnk.sys, fildds.sys are three specific vulnerable drivers explicitly named in the Acronis writeup as INC's BYOVD toolkit. None are part of any mainstream commercial product, so any load is high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher reproducing the BYOVD chain in a malware-analysis VM
  • Red-team engagement using a leaked INC affiliate toolkit
  • Backup/storage product that legitimately ships one of these driver names (verify the SHA256 against vendor catalogue first)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe", "MsSense.exe")) and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\drivers\" and InitiatingProcessAccountName == "system" and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "services.exe" and SHA256 in (dynamic([])))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull SHA256 of the loaded .sys, look up signer/age; check whether host has a paired Defender 'Impair Defenses' or service-stop alert in the prior 15 minutes. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the device via Defender Live Response; capture memory image before reboot; block driver hash tenant-wide via Defender ASR vulnerable-driver list (or WDAC) and quarantine the .sys file. 3) HUNT: Pivot on InitiatingProcessFolderPath for parent dropper, then search for ScreenConnect/AnyDesk/TeamViewer installs, rclone.exe activity, and access to Veeam backup shares from the same host in the prior 24h to find the affiliate's full chain.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("DriverLoad", "AsrVulnerableSignedDriverAudited", "AsrVulnerableSignedDriverBlocked")
| where FileName in~ ("filwfp.sys", "filnk.sys", "fildds.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 6
| where ParameterXml has_any ("filwfp.sys", "filnk.sys", "fildds.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, ParameterXml
| order by TimeGenerated desc

INC Rust encryptor invoked with --esxi VM-shutdown flag AIActions on Objectives High
Detects any process execution carrying the '--esxi' command-line argument, which is the documented INC ransomware Rust encryptor switch that shuts down virtual machines before encryption on Linux/ESXi hosts (and observed on Windows when staged from a jump box). This argument is not a standard flag for any benign Windows utility. Rationale: '--esxi' is explicitly called out as INC's encryptor argument that triggers VM shutdown. The token is highly unusual in normal command-line traffic — no Microsoft, VMware, or RMM utility uses it natively.
ATT&CKT1486 T1489
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal IR/purple-team exercise running a captured INC sample in a lab subnet
  • VMware/ESXi admin scripts that happen to pass '--esxi' as a custom argument to in-house tooling
  • Security testing of the YARA/sandbox pipeline replaying INC payload metadata
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\IR-Sandbox\", @"\malware-analysis\")) and not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe") and FolderPath startswith @"C:\Tools\IR\")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and SHA256; correlate to any vssadmin/wmic shadow-copy deletion, BYOVD driver load, or RMM tool install on the same host in the prior 60 minutes. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host immediately via EDR network containment; snapshot the system; if multiple hosts hit simultaneously, declare incident and block the binary hash tenant-wide. 3) HUNT: Search for the same binary SHA256 across the estate, look for rclone exfil and 7-Zip/WinRAR archive staging on file servers, and enumerate VMware/ESXi management VLAN authentications from compromised credentials in the last 7 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--esxi"
| where not(AccountName endswith "$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "--esxi"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rclone exfiltration to cloud-storage remote (INC double-extortion staging) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects execution of rclone.exe with cloud-storage remote arguments (mega:, drive:, s3:, b2:, dropbox:) and copy/sync verbs, matching INC affiliates' documented pattern of exfiltrating password-protected archives before encryption. Pairs the binary name with the cloud-remote token to avoid firing on legitimate admin file-sync. Rationale: Article names rclone as INC's exfil tool for password-protected archives. Pairing the binary name with copy/sync verbs AND cloud-remote tokens eliminates legitimate rclone hash/version checks while keeping the exfil signal sharp.
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1048
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup admin running scheduled rclone job to legitimate S3/B2 bucket (whitelist by service account + scheduled-task parent)
  • Data engineer pushing dataset to Drive/Dropbox via approved sync workflow
  • Developer using rclone interactively during testing from a dev jump-box
  • MSP-managed backup product wrapping rclone internally
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe", "Veeam.Agent.exe")) and not(AccountName in~ ("svc-backup", "svc-rclone"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Extract the rclone remote name and config path from CommandLine; resolve the destination endpoint from --config file or DNS lookups; check egress bytes from EDR/firewall in the prior 4 hours. 2) CONTAIN: Block destination domain/IP at perimeter, isolate the host, kill the rclone process tree, snapshot %APPDATA%\rclone\rclone.conf to recover the access-key. 3) HUNT: Search for 7z.exe / WinRAR.exe staging of password-protected archives in the prior 24h, enumerate file-server access by the same user (look for crawl patterns over SMB), and check Defender FileEvents for archive creation in C:\Users\Public, C:\ProgramData, or \Windows\Temp.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName =~ "rclone.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has "rclone" or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "rclone.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" copy ", " sync ", " move ", " lsd ", " lsf ")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("mega:", "drive:", "s3:", "b2:", "dropbox:", "onedrive:", "box:", "--remote", "--config")
| where not(AccountName endswith "$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rclone.exe" or CommandLine has "rclone"
| where CommandLine has_any (" copy ", " sync ", " move ")
| where CommandLine has_any ("mega:", "drive:", "s3:", "b2:", "dropbox:", "onedrive:", "box:", "--remote", "--config")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
