WordPress site serving injected SocGholish loader to internal browser AIDelivery Medium
Detects internal browser HTTP/HTTPS GETs that retrieve injected JavaScript loaders matching the SocGholish profile from WordPress-hosted paths (wp-content, wp-includes, wp-admin) — the drive-by staging step described in the article. Pivots on the wp-* URL fragment + script Content-Type returning to a non-script-expecting referer. Rationale: Article's central claim is '14,971 compromised WordPress websites' delivering SocGholish via injected JS. The wp-content/wp-includes URL surface plus browser UA plus .js retrieval is the article-specific delivery shape. We avoid hardcoding domains because Operation Endgame just disinfected the known ones — the *next* compromised WP site will look identical at the URL-pattern layer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/are-you-sure-your-browser-up-date-current-landscape-fake-browser-updates • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189/
ATT&CKT1189 T1584.006
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WordPress-hosted marketing sites with JS analytics
  • Corporate blog on WordPress legitimately serving JS theme/plugin assets
  • Internal WordPress intranet sites with JS plugins
  • Cookie-consent banners loaded from wp-content
  • Third-party WordPress vendor docs sites accessed for research
Suppression filter
and not RemoteUrl has_any ("/wp-content/themes/","/wp-content/plugins/jetpack/","/wp-includes/js/jquery/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dedupe by URL+domain and run the resolved domain through URLhaus, abuse.ch ThreatFox, and the Operation Endgame seizure list — Dutch NHTCU publishes seized domains post-operation. 2) Contain: if any URL is confirmed malicious, block the FQDN at proxy/firewall and pivot to every host that visited it. 3) Hunt: for confirmed-bad URLs, search DeviceProcessEvents on the visiting host(s) for wscript/cscript children of the browser within 10 minutes — that's the executed SocGholish chain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/wp-content/","/wp-includes/","/wp-admin/admin-ajax.php","/wp-json/")
| where RemoteUrl endswith ".js" or RemoteUrl has ".js?" or RemoteUrl has "=eval"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), HostsHit = dcount(DeviceName), Hits = count() by RemoteUrl, tostring(split(RemoteUrl,"/")[2])
| where HostsHit >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("Chrome","Edg","Firefox","Brave")
| where Url has_any ("/wp-content/","/wp-includes/","/wp-admin/admin-ajax.php","/wp-json/")
| where Url endswith ".js" or Url has ".js?" or Url contains "=eval"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), HostsHit = dcount(SrcHostname), Hits = count() by Url, DstHostname
| where HostsHit >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:(zscaler OR proxy OR squid OR bluecoat) @http.url:(*\/wp-content\/* OR *\/wp-includes\/* OR *\/wp-admin\/admin-ajax.php* OR *\/wp-json\/*) @http.url:(*.js* OR *eval*) @http.useragent:(*Chrome* OR *Edg* OR *Firefox* OR *Brave*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|opera)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
| sort(count, order=asc)
| count<=2
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url LIKE "%/wp-content/%" OR Web.url LIKE "%/wp-includes/%" OR Web.url LIKE "%/wp-admin/%" OR Web.url LIKE "%/wp-json/%" by Web.src Web.user Web.url Web.url_domain Web.http_user_agent Web.http_referrer Web.http_content_type | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where like(url, "%.js%") AND (like(http_content_type, "%javascript%") OR like(http_content_type, "%text/html%")) | stats count dc(src) as host_count values(url) as urls by url_domain | where host_count >= 1
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url LIKE "%/wp-content/%" OR Web.url LIKE "%/wp-includes/%" OR Web.url LIKE "%/wp-admin/%" OR Web.url LIKE "%/wp-json/%" by Web.src Web.user Web.url Web.url_domain Web.http_user_agent Web.http_referrer Web.http_content_type | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where like(url, "%.js%") AND (like(http_content_type, "%javascript%") OR like(http_content_type, "%text/html%")) | stats count dc(src) as host_count values(url) as urls by url_domain | where host_count >= 1
Script interpreter spawning PE loader after browser-delivered JS (SocGholish second stage) AIInstallation High
Detects wscript.exe/cscript.exe spawning a PE child (rundll32, regsvr32, powershell, or a written-then-executed binary in AppData) — the SocGholish hand-off to Dridex/Empire/Koadic/Azorult/Chthonic that the article explicitly names. Filters on the wscript-parent chain so it doesn't fire on legit admin scripting. Rationale: Article calls out the loader explicitly: 'SocGholish has also been used to deploy other malware families, including Dridex, Doppelpaymer, Empire, Koadic, Chtonic, and Azorult.' That deployment universally requires wscript/cscript to spawn a follow-on process. The parent .js requirement strips legit admin scripts that don't go through a JS file. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0760/ • https://redcanary.com/threat-detection-report/threats/socgholish/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.001 T1218.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy enterprise install wrappers using cscript to drive PowerShell setup steps
  • SCCM/MECM script-based deployment phases
  • Custom internal automation: JS launcher chaining to rundll32 for COM registration
  • Adobe / Java updater chains using script host as intermediate
  • Corporate logon scripts spawning powershell for inventory
Suppression filter
and not InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","msiexec.exe","taskeng.exe") and not InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sccm-deploy","intune-package")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the spawned child's SHA256 and command line, plus the parent wscript's CommandLine — the .js path/URL gives you the originating compromised WP site. Run the binary hash through MDE/VT. 2) Contain: isolate the device, kill the wscript tree, quarantine any new PE written to AppData/Public, reset the user's session and AD creds (SocGholish loaders frequently steal Dridex-style banking creds). 3) Hunt: pivot on the JS file path/SHA across the fleet to find peers infected from the same compromised WordPress page, and run the shadow-copy-deletion UC on every confirmed host — Evil Corp commonly chains to WastedLocker/Phoenix CryptoLocker from this same chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","cmd.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wmic.exe")
   or (FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Public\") and FileName endswith ".exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          GrandparentImage = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","cmd.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wmic.exe")
   or (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Public\") and ActingProcessName endswith ".exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SocGholish Script-to-PE Hand-Off (Second Stage Loader)
id: 4b8e1f23-a712-4d50-b1a0-3c4d5e6f7a8b
description: Detects wscript.exe/cscript.exe spawning a PE loader (powershell, rundll32, regsvr32, mshta, cmd, bitsadmin, certutil, curl, wmic) - the SocGholish hand-off to second-stage payloads (Dridex, Empire, Koadic, Azorult, Chthonic).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/law-enforcement-nukes-socgholish-malware-from-nearly-15-000-sites/
  - https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0760/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1218.011
  - attack.execution
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
    ParentCommandLine|contains: '.js'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wmic.exe'
  condition: all of selection_*
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate corporate JS installers chaining to PowerShell post-install steps
  - Software-deployment helpers using cscript to drive an MSI
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) @ParentImage:(*\wscript.exe OR *\WScript.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\CScript.exe) @ParentCommandLine:*.js* @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\rundll32.exe OR *\Rundll32.exe OR *\regsvr32.exe OR *\RegSvr32.exe OR *\mshta.exe OR *\MSHTA.EXE OR *\bitsadmin.exe OR *\certutil.exe OR *\CertUtil.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh|rundll32|regsvr32|mshta|bitsadmin|certutil|curl|wmic)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","cmd.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","cmd.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Shadow copy deletion within 24h of SocGholish script execution (Evil Corp ransomware prelude) AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates a vssadmin/wmic/PowerShell shadow-copy deletion with a prior wscript-from-browser execution on the same host within 24h — the SocGholish→Evil Corp ransomware hand-off pattern named in the article (WastedLocker, Hades, Macaw, Phoenix CryptoLocker). This is the article's stated end-state impact. Rationale: Article explicitly attributes the chain to Evil Corp's ransomware history: 'was behind the WastedLocker, Hades, Macaw Locker, and Phoenix CryptoLocker ransomware operations.' All those families delete VSS shadow copies before encrypting; correlating that with the SocGholish script execution on the same host within 24h gives an extremely high-confidence end-stage detection. Cross-checked Mandiant's WastedLocker analysis and CISA AA22-264A which describe the exact vssadmin+bcdedit prep pattern used post-SocGholish. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-264a • https://www.mandiant.com/resources/blog/wastedlocker-ransomware-evil-corp • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0037/
ATT&CKT1490 T1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/Veritas pre-backup shadow-copy cleanup on the same host that ran a legit corporate JS deployment
  • Sysadmin manually troubleshooting VSS on a workstation that earlier ran a corporate JS installer
  • Windows Update / DISM operations clearing shadows post-cumulative update
  • ConfigMgr OS deployment task sequences calling vssadmin
  • SQL Server pre-snapshot maintenance jobs
Suppression filter
and not (VssCmd has_any ("veeam","sql","DISM","sccm","intune") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","sqlservr.exe","tiworker.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is treated as a ransomware-in-progress incident — pull the wscript .js path, the vssadmin/bcdedit cmdline, and the spawning user, and cross-check the host for file-rename storms in DeviceFileEvents during the same window. 2) Contain: isolate immediately (Defender 'Isolate device' / Falcon Network Containment), suspend the user across AD and EntraID, kill all child processes of wscript, and block the originating compromised WP domain at proxy/firewall. Alert IR leadership and engage Evil Corp playbook (WastedLocker/Phoenix CryptoLocker). 3) Hunt: pivot on the user/host across the fleet for lateral movement (SMB writes, WMI exec, PsExec) in the prior 6h; look for the originating compromised WordPress URL in proxy logs across the org and quarantine every host that visited it.
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let Scripts = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where AccountName !endswith "$"
  | where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
  | where ProcessCommandLine has ".js"
  | project ScriptTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, ScriptCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
   or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Win32_Shadowcopy","Remove-WmiObject Win32_Shadowcopy","Get-WmiObject Win32_Shadowcopy"))
   or (FileName =~ "bcdedit.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("recoveryenabled no","bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures"))
| join kind=inner Scripts on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (ScriptTime .. ScriptTime + LookbackHours)
| project ScriptTime, VssTime = Timestamp,
          DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, ScriptTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, ScriptCmd,
          VssBinary = FileName, VssCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by VssTime desc
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let Scripts = ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
  | where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
  | where ParentProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has ".js"
  | project ScriptTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ScriptCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (ActingProcessName has "vssadmin.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
   or (ActingProcessName has "wmic.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
   or (ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Win32_Shadowcopy","Remove-WmiObject Win32_Shadowcopy"))
   or (ActingProcessName has "bcdedit.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("recoveryenabled no","bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures"))
| join kind=inner Scripts on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (ScriptTime .. ScriptTime + LookbackHours)
| project ScriptTime, VssTime = TimeGenerated,
          DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, ScriptTime),
          DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ScriptCmd,
          VssBinary = ActingProcessName, VssCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by VssTime desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) ((@Image:(*\vssadmin.exe OR *\VSSAdmin.exe OR *\VSSADMIN.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*delete* AND *shadows*)) OR (@Image:(*\wmic.exe OR *\WMIC.exe) AND @CommandLine:(*shadowcopy* AND *delete*)) OR (@Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe) AND @CommandLine:(*Win32_Shadowcopy* OR *Remove-WmiObject*Shadowcopy*)) OR (@Image:(*\bcdedit.exe OR *\BCDEdit.exe) AND @CommandLine:(*recoveryenabled?no* OR *bootstatuspolicy?ignoreallfailures*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\\vssadmin\.exe$/i AND regex("(?i)delete\\s+shadows", field=CommandLine))
  OR (ImageFileName=/\\wmic\.exe$/i AND regex("(?i)shadowcopy", field=CommandLine) AND regex("(?i)delete", field=CommandLine))
  OR (ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i AND regex("(?i)Win32_Shadowcopy", field=CommandLine))
  OR (ImageFileName=/\\bcdedit\.exe$/i AND regex("(?i)recoveryenabled\\s+no|bootstatuspolicy\\s+ignoreallfailures", field=CommandLine))
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | ParentBaseFileName=/^(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave)\.exe$/i | ImageFileName=/\\(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i | regex("\\.js", field=CommandLine)}, field=aid, include=[ComputerName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as scriptTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe") AND Processes.process LIKE "%.js%" by Processes.dest Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | join type=inner dest [| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as vssTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="vssadmin.exe" AND Processes.process LIKE "%delete shadows%") OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process LIKE "%shadowcopy%" AND Processes.process LIKE "%delete%") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND (Processes.process LIKE "%Win32_Shadowcopy%" AND Processes.process LIKE "%Remove%")) by Processes.dest Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | rename process as vss_cmd] | eval delta=vssTime-scriptTime | where delta>=0 AND delta<=86400 | table scriptTime vssTime delta dest user vss_cmd
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as scriptTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe") AND Processes.process LIKE "%.js%" by Processes.dest Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | join type=inner dest [| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as vssTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="vssadmin.exe" AND Processes.process LIKE "%delete shadows%") OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process LIKE "%shadowcopy%" AND Processes.process LIKE "%delete%") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND (Processes.process LIKE "%Win32_Shadowcopy%" AND Processes.process LIKE "%Remove%")) by Processes.dest Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | rename process as vss_cmd] | eval delta=vssTime-scriptTime | where delta>=0 AND delta<=86400 | table scriptTime vssTime delta dest user vss_cmd
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/

    - attack.credential-access

    category: process_access
    product: windows

        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'

        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] LicenseLoader.php dropped into WordPress plugins directory · [LLM] Fake woocommerce-subscription / woocommerce-notification plugin directory created
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ShapedPlugin backdoor C2 beacon to generate.2faplugin.org / 194.76.217.28 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
ShapedPlugin backdoor C2 beacon to generate.2faplugin.org / 194.76.217.28 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts WordPress hosts beaconing to the ShapedPlugin supply-chain backdoor C2 (generate.2faplugin.org / 194.76.217.28) — the LicenseLoader.php stager contacts this infrastructure when a WP admin first accesses the panel, then again to register the implant. Article-specific via the unique C2 domain and IP confirmed by Wordfence. Rationale: Locks on the exact second-stage C2 domain (generate.2faplugin.org) and IP (194.76.217.28) named in Wordfence's analysis of the ShapedPlugin compromise. Cross-checked via the BleepingComputer write-up and the article's pre-extracted IOC list. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/shapedplugin-update-flow-hacked-to-infect-wordpress-sites/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher sandboxing the malicious plugin in a lab
  • WAF/threat-intel feed crawler proactively probing the IOC
  • DNS-based threat-intel platforms (e.g. URLScan, VirusTotal nodes) resolving the domain for enrichment
  • Internal SOC re-validation traffic from a known jump-host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("urlscan.exe","vt-cli.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("soc-research","threat-intel")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source host is a WordPress webserver and identify the PHP process / cron job that originated the egress; pull wp-content/plugins/ listing for LicenseLoader.php and any woocommerce-subscription / woocommerce-notification directories. 2) Contain: block 194.76.217.28 and *.2faplugin.org at egress + WAF, isolate the webserver from the database VLAN, and force-rotate all WordPress admin passwords, 2FA secrets, wp-config.php AUTH keys, DB and SMTP credentials. 3) Hunt: scan all WP estates for the three affected plugins (Product Slider Pro <3.5.4, Real Testimonials Pro 3.2.5, Smart Post Show Pro <4.0.2), search file writes for LicenseLoader.php across all hosts, and review the last 90 days of WooCommerce order exports for exfil indicators.
let C2Domain = "2faplugin.org";
let C2IP = "194.76.217.28";
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has C2Domain or RemoteIP == C2IP
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Domain = "2faplugin.org";
let C2IP = "194.76.217.28";
let DnsHits =
    ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DnsQuery has C2Domain
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = coalesce(DvcHostname, SrcHostname), SrcIp = SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, Vendor = EventVendor, Product = EventProduct;
let NetHits =
    ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DstIpAddr == C2IP or DstHostname has C2Domain or Url has C2Domain
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = coalesce(DvcHostname, SrcHostname), SrcIp = SrcIpAddr, DstIp = DstIpAddr, DstHost = DstHostname, Url, Vendor = EventVendor, Product = EventProduct;
let ProxyHits =
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DestinationHostName has C2Domain or DestinationIP == C2IP or RequestURL has C2Domain
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = SourceHostName, SrcIp = SourceIP, DstIp = DestinationIP, DstHost = DestinationHostName, Url = RequestURL, Vendor = DeviceVendor, Product = DeviceProduct;
union isfuzzy=true DnsHits, NetHits, ProxyHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LicenseLoader.php dropped into WordPress plugins directory AIInstallation High
Hunts the creation of the ShapedPlugin supply-chain stager file (LicenseLoader.php) inside a wp-content/plugins/ subdirectory. The file is injected into the Product Slider Pro, Real Testimonials Pro and Smart Post Show Pro Pro builds and self-deletes after staging — catching the write is the highest-fidelity host-side signal. Rationale: LicenseLoader.php is the specific stager filename Wordfence named in the ShapedPlugin compromise; the wp-content/plugins path constraint anchors it to a real WordPress install and avoids matching unrelated PHP files. Sourced from the BleepingComputer article body. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/shapedplugin-update-flow-hacked-to-infect-wordpress-sites/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer testing a custom plugin licensing system named LicenseLoader.php
  • Restore from backup that re-introduces the file on a previously-infected host
  • Security researcher staging IOCs in a sandbox
  • Plugin auditor scanning compromised plugin payloads in a dedicated review environment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("sec-research","plugin-auditor") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--lab-restore"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the file hash, confirm the parent plugin directory matches one of Product Slider Pro / Real Testimonials Pro / Smart Post Show Pro, and identify the PHP-FPM or web user that wrote the file. 2) Contain: quarantine LicenseLoader.php and the parent plugin directory, isolate the host from the DB VLAN, and pull wp-config.php for exposure review (AUTH keys, DB creds). 3) Hunt: search for follow-on writes to wp-content/plugins/woocommerce-subscription/ and woocommerce-notification/, review wp_users for rogue admin additions in the past 30 days, and pivot on the file SHA256 across the estate.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "LicenseLoader.php"
| where FolderPath has "wp-content" and FolderPath has "plugins"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName =~ "LicenseLoader.php"
| where TargetFilePath has "wp-content" and TargetFilePath has "plugins"
| project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake woocommerce-subscription / woocommerce-notification plugin directory created AIInstallation High
Hunts the installation of the second-stage fake plugin used by the ShapedPlugin backdoor, which masquerades as 'woocommerce-subscription' or 'woocommerce-notification' under wp-content/plugins/ and is hidden from the WordPress plugin list. These specific names are the article's named impersonation strings. Rationale: The two fake plugin slugs (woocommerce-subscription and woocommerce-notification) are the exact names Wordfence and BleepingComputer published for the second-stage impersonation directories — genuine WooCommerce subscription/notification plugins use different slugs, so creation of these specific directory names is a near-binary indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/shapedplugin-update-flow-hacked-to-infect-wordpress-sites/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Site admin manually creating a custom plugin folder using the same name (rare — these slugs are not WooCommerce-official)
  • Restore of a previously-infected WordPress backup
  • Researcher reproducing the IOC in a sandbox
  • Misnamed in-house WooCommerce integration plugin
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("sec-research","backup-restore")
Response runbook
1) Triage: list every file under the fake plugin directory, hash each PHP file, and check whether the plugin appears in wp-admin's plugin list (article notes it is hidden) by inspecting wp_options / active_plugins. 2) Contain: delete the rogue directory, force-rotate all WordPress admin and database credentials plus wp-config.php AUTH/SECURE keys and SMTP creds, and revoke any newly issued WP REST API application passwords. 3) Hunt: query the past 90 days of WooCommerce order exports for evidence of bulk exfil, audit wp_users for unknown admin-role additions, and search for outbound traffic to 194.76.217.28 / *.2faplugin.org across the estate.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("wp-content/plugins/woocommerce-subscription","wp-content\\plugins\\woocommerce-subscription","wp-content/plugins/woocommerce-notification","wp-content\\plugins\\woocommerce-notification")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("wp-content/plugins/woocommerce-subscription","wp-content\\plugins\\woocommerce-subscription","wp-content/plugins/woocommerce-notification","wp-content\\plugins\\woocommerce-notification")
| project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

description: |

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FortiGate SSL VPN authentication brute-force burst (FortiBleed harvesting campaign) · [LLM] Microsoft SQL Server brute-force burst correlated with FortiBleed operator MO
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] FortiGate SSL VPN successful login from anonymizer/new-geography post-FortiBleed · [LLM] FortiGate management/admin portal login success from public internet source
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
FortiGate SSL VPN successful login from anonymizer/new-geography post-FortiBleed AIExploitation High
Hunts for successful FortiGate SSL VPN authentications from IPs/countries the user has never authenticated from before — the expected access pattern after the FortiBleed dataset of 73,932 firewall URLs with plaintext credentials gets weaponised. Article-specific because affected orgs are named (Chevron, Samsung, Foxconn, Comcast, AT&T, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota, Sinopec, State Grid) and Beaumont confirmed the creds are live. Rationale: The article + Beaumont/Hudson Rock corroboration confirms 73,932 FortiGate URLs with plaintext SSL VPN credentials are live. Detecting a successful SSL VPN auth from an IP the user has never used before is the cleanest indicator of leaked-cred reuse. The CommonSecurityLog connector is Microsoft's recommended Fortinet path (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/sentinel/data-connectors/fortinet-fortigate-next-generation-firewall). Cross-checked against: • https://www.kevinbeaumont.com/ • https://www.hudsonrock.com/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/sentinel/data-connectors/fortinet-fortigate-next-generation-firewall
ATT&CKT1078 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication Network_Sessions.All_Sessions
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user traveling and connecting from hotel/airport Wi-Fi for the first time
  • Mobile workers with carrier-grade NAT IPs that rotate weekly
  • Newly hired employee's first VPN connection
  • Vendor / contractor connecting from their own corporate IP for the first time
  • Disaster-recovery / failover routing the VPN client to a different egress
Suppression filter
| where SrcCountry !in ("<list-of-employee-travel-countries>") or DestinationUserName !in (dynamic(["<known-mobile-workers>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DestinationUserName + SourceIP, geo-locate, confirm with the user via out-of-band channel that they initiated the session. Check baseline ASN/country vs the new one. 2) Contain: if unconfirmed, force-disconnect the SSL VPN session on the FortiGate (`diag sys session clear`), invalidate the user's password, revoke active tokens, and require MFA re-enrollment. Block the source IP at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SourceIP across all FortiGate, AAD, and ImAuthentication tables for 30 days; pivot on DestinationUserName for any internal lateral-movement signals (RDP / SMB / Kerberos TGS), and check whether the user appears in the Hudson Rock FortiBleed lookup.
// FortiGate SSL VPN logs typically arrive via 3rd-party MDE connector or surface in DeviceLogonEvents only when the VPN client logs onto the endpoint. Best-effort: surface RemoteInteractive/Network logons immediately preceded by VPN client connect, from non-corp IPs.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let KnownCorpSubnets = dynamic(["10.","172.16.","172.17.","172.18.","172.19.","172.20.","172.21.","172.22.","172.23.","172.24.","172.25.","172.26.","172.27.","172.28.","172.29.","172.30.","172.31.","192.168."]);
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
| where LogonType in ("RemoteInteractive","Network")
| where isnotempty(RemoteIP) and RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where not(RemoteIP startswith_cs KnownCorpSubnets[0])
| join kind=leftanti (
    DeviceLogonEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(60d) .. ago(LookbackDays))
    | where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
    | summarize by AccountName, RemoteIP
) on AccountName, RemoteIP
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountDomain, LogonType, RemoteIP, RemoteDeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// FortiGate sends CEF/syslog to CommonSecurityLog (Fortinet AzMonitor connector)
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let BaselineDays = 60d;
let Baseline =
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(BaselineDays) .. ago(LookbackDays))
    | where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
    | where DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
    | where Activity has_any ("ssl vpn login","sslvpn-login","sslvpn_session_user_login_event")
    | where DeviceAction =~ "login" or Message has "login successfully"
    | summarize by DestinationHostName, SourceIP;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
| where Activity has_any ("ssl vpn login","sslvpn-login","sslvpn_session_user_login_event")
| where DeviceAction =~ "login" or Message has "login successfully"
| where isnotempty(DestinationHostName) and isnotempty(SourceIP)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on DestinationHostName, SourceIP
| extend GeoIP = geo_info_from_ip_address(SourceIP)
| extend SrcCountry = tostring(GeoIP.country)
| project TimeGenerated, User=DestinationHostName, SourceIP, SrcCountry, DeviceName=DestinationHostName, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FortiGate SSL VPN authentication brute-force burst (FortiBleed harvesting campaign) AIDelivery High
Detects high-volume failed SSL VPN authentication attempts against FortiGate from a single source IP — the exact behavior Diachenko reported (1.16 billion credential attempts against 320,777 FortiGate targets). Threshold-based count over a 10-minute window per source IP, matching the operator-scale brute-force campaign harvesting these credentials. Rationale: Diachenko's investigation enumerated 1.16B credential attempts across 320,777 FortiGate targets — a brute-force pattern that produces a clear high-volume failed-auth burst signature in FortiGate event logs. 50 failures/10min from one IP is well above legitimate fat-finger behavior. CommonSecurityLog DestinationUserName/SourceIP are the canonical CEF fields. Cross-checked against: • https://www.hudsonrock.com/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/sentinel/data-connectors/fortinet-fortigate-next-generation-firewall
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1110.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Misconfigured FortiClient on a laptop with stale cached credentials looping
  • Penetration testing engagement against the FortiGate
  • RADIUS / LDAP backend outage causing valid auth to register as failure
  • Stale service account in a script repeatedly attempting connection
  • Vulnerability scanner enumerating SSL VPN response codes
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<known-pentest-ips>","<vuln-scanner-ips>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is external; check SampleUsers for password-spray pattern (many users) vs single-user brute-force; geo-IP the source. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the perimeter and FortiGate's quarantine list, enable lockout policy if not active, force password rotation on any accounts that subsequently authenticated successfully from that IP. 3) Hunt: pivot the SourceIP across 30 days for any successful login from the same source; cross-check the impacted FortiGate's external URL against the Hudson Rock FortiBleed lookup tool to determine prior exposure.
// FortiGate brute-force telemetry is not natively in MDE. Best-effort proxy: outbound public IPs touching VPN endpoints from EDR perspective is not the right surface. Use sentinel_kql instead.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 443
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("FortiClient.exe","FortiSSLVPNdaemon.exe")
| summarize Attempts=count() by RemoteIP, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where Attempts > 30
| order by Timestamp desc
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
let AttemptThreshold = 50;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
| where Activity has_any ("ssl vpn login fail","sslvpn-login-fail","ssl_vpn_login_fail")
   or Message has_any ("ssl_login_fail","sslvpn_login_fail","login failed")
| summarize Attempts=count(),
            UniqueUsers=dcount(DestinationHostName),
            SampleUsers=make_set(DestinationHostName, 10)
            by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMinutes)
| where Attempts >= AttemptThreshold
| extend GeoIP = geo_info_from_ip_address(SourceIP), SrcCountry = tostring(GeoIP.country)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft SQL Server brute-force burst correlated with FortiBleed operator MO AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for high-volume failed SQL Server authentication attempts (event 18456) against internet-exposed MSSQL — Diachenko reported the same operators conducted 2.1 billion credential attempts against 163,650 MSSQL targets alongside the FortiGate campaign. Detection is specific because it threshold-correlates failed SQL logon counts the way the operators ran them in parallel with the FortiGate campaign. Rationale: Article explicitly quantifies 2.1B SQL Server credential attempts against 163,650 MSSQL hosts conducted by the same operators. EventID 18456 is the canonical SQL auth-failure ID and the SecurityEvent / SQL ERRORLOG fields are well-defined. Threshold of 100/10min cleanly separates this from app-tier connection-pool churn. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/relational-databases/errors-events/mssqlserver-18456-database-engine-error • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fortibleed-leak-exposes-fortinet-vpn-credentials-for-73-000-devices/
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1110.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • App tier with rotated credentials looping reconnection attempts
  • Sysadmin running sqlcmd with wrong password while troubleshooting
  • DBA toolset (DBeaver/SSMS) connecting to retired instance with old creds
  • Vulnerability scanner enumerating MSSQL versions
  • Failover cluster transient auth churn during AG failover
Suppression filter
| where IpAddress !in (dynamic(["<app-tier-subnets>"])) and Computer !startswith "AG-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check IpAddress source — internal app servers warrant a credential-rotation conversation, external IPs warrant block-first; review SampleAccounts for sa/admin enumeration. 2) Contain: block external SourceIP at perimeter, disable SQL Server Authentication on internet-exposed instances if not required, force `sa` password rotation, enable account lockout. 3) Hunt: pivot the IpAddress across 30 days for successful SQL auth, check for follow-on xp_cmdshell, SQLCLR, or BCP/openrowset abuse, and confirm whether the SQL host is also a FortiGate-protected segment listed in the FortiBleed dataset.

FortiGate management/admin portal login success from public internet source AIExploitation Medium
Detects successful FortiGate administrative GUI / SSH / API authentication where the source IP is on the public internet — the exact exposure Beaumont called out ("a majority of the affected devices expose their FortiGate management interfaces directly to the internet"). Pairs the leaked admin credentials in the FortiBleed dataset with the misconfiguration that lets them be used remotely. Rationale: Beaumont's analysis (cited in the article) confirms that a majority of the 73k+ affected FortiGate devices have management interfaces exposed to the public internet, and the FortiBleed dataset contains admin credentials extracted from FortiGate configs. Successful admin authentication from a non-RFC1918 source is a high-fidelity indicator that a leaked credential is being used. CommonSecurityLog columns used (DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Activity, DeviceAction, SourceIP, DestinationUserName, DestinationHostName, Message) are all canonical CEF fields for the Fortinet connector. Cross-checked against: • https://www.kevinbeaumont.com/ • https://www.hudsonrock.com/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/sentinel/data-connectors/fortinet-fortigate-next-generation-firewall
ATT&CKT1078 T1133 T1556
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network engineer working from home over residential ISP without site-to-site VPN
  • MSP / Fortinet partner managing the firewall from their own corporate IP
  • Fortinet TAC / professional services session over public Internet
  • Out-of-band administrative session during a site-to-site VPN outage
  • Cloud-hosted FortiGate (Azure / AWS) where mgmt interface is intentionally public and ACL'd
Suppression filter
| where AdminUser !in (dynamic(["<MSP-admin-name>","fortinet-tac"])) and SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<MSP-egress-ips>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull SourceIP, geo-locate, and confirm via change-management whether the engineer scheduled an out-of-band admin session; review the FortiGate's `config system admin` trusthost ACL to see whether the source was allow-listed. 2) Contain: if unconfirmed, force-disconnect the admin session, rotate every admin credential on the device (`config system admin` + `set password`), restrict mgmt-interface access to trusthost CIDRs only, and enable MFA on admin accounts. 3) Hunt: pivot SourceIP across all FortiGate logs for 30 days for config-change events (`config system`, `config firewall policy`); check the FortiGate's configuration for unauthorized backdoor admin accounts or VPN portals; verify the device's external URL against Hudson Rock's FortiBleed lookup tool.
// FortiGate admin-portal auth does not surface on Defender XDR; CommonSecurityLog (Sentinel) is the right pivot. Best-effort EDR proxy: outbound HTTPS/SSH from admin workstations to FortiGate management IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (22, 443, 8443)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("putty.exe","plink.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
| where Activity has_any ("admin login","admin_login_success","login","login successful")
   or Message has_any ("User admin login successfully","login succeeded from","Administrator","logged in successfully")
| where isnotempty(SourceIP)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| extend GeoIP = geo_info_from_ip_address(SourceIP), SrcCountry = tostring(GeoIP.country)
| project TimeGenerated,
          AdminUser = coalesce(DestinationHostName, SourceUserName),
          FortiGate = DestinationHostName,
          SourceIP,
          SrcCountry,
          Activity,
          DeviceAction,
          Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable NGINX versions exposed to CVE-2026-42530 / CVE-2026-42055 AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts running NGINX builds Defender TVM flags as affected by the June 2026 out-of-band F5 advisory. Targets the inventory layer so we can prioritise patching of NGINX Plus / OSS / Gateway Fabric / Instance Manager before exploitation begins. Rationale: Article explicitly names CVE-2026-42530 (ngx_http_v3_module), CVE-2026-42055 (proxy_v2 / grpc), and the two Gateway Fabric flaws CVE-2026-11311 / CVE-2026-50107. Pivot to TVM gives a high-fidelity asset list before any in-the-wild exploitation kicks off.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM lag where a host patched within the last sync interval still appears
  • Stale inventory entries for decommissioned NGINX containers/sidecars
  • Vendor-renamed packages (e.g. distro-built nginx-core) that TVM tags with the upstream CveId even after backported fix
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "0.0.0" and isnotempty(RecommendedSecurityUpdate)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SoftwareVersion is below the F5 advisory's fixed builds for the specific edition (Plus / OSS / Gateway Fabric / Instance Manager) and check whether the host is internet-facing (DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing) or fronting sensitive backends. 2) Contain: for CVE-2026-42530 push the config workaround (remove `quic` from all `listen` directives) and for CVE-2026-42055 remove `ignore_invalid_headers off` and drop `large_client_header_buffers` below 2 MB until packages are upgraded. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same hosts to UC2 (worker crashes) and UC3 (oversized headers) to verify no pre-patch exploitation; check change tickets for unexpected NGINX config diffs (CVE-2026-11311 / 50107).

NGINX worker process abnormal restart fan-out (CVE-2026-42530 / 42055 post-exploit crash signal) AIExploitation Medium
Both critical CVEs cause a use-after-free or heap overflow that restarts the NGINX worker. A burst of worker exits-on-signal across hosts is the cheapest behavioural tell that someone is probing or weaponising the bugs against your fleet. Rationale: Article says "successful exploitation causes a use-after-free or heap-based buffer overflow in the NGINX worker process, leading to a restart." That is the load-bearing observable — a spike of worker exits on SIGSEGV/SIGABRT is the cheapest way to detect mass-exploit probing before vendor IOCs land.
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate `nginx -s reload` after a config push (parent=root, signal=15 not 11)
  • OOM-killer terminating workers under memory pressure (look for cgroup/oom kill in same log)
  • Misconfigured upstream causing repeated worker timeouts but no signal crash
  • Auto-scaled container restarts under k8s liveness probe failures
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "signal 15" and SyslogMessage !has "graceful shutdown"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the signal is 11 (SIGSEGV) or 6 (SIGABRT), not 15 (graceful reload); pull the nginx error.log around the crash window for the upstream module name — if `quic` / `http3` appears it's CVE-2026-42530, if `proxy_v2` / `grpc` appears it's CVE-2026-42055. 2) Contain: apply the article's config workarounds immediately (remove `quic` from `listen` directives; remove `ignore_invalid_headers off` and lower `large_client_header_buffers` below 2 MB); throttle the source IPs that preceded the crash via WAF. 3) Hunt: pivot on `RequestClientApplication` / `cs(User-Agent)` and `c-ip` from W3CIISLog / CommonSecurityLog 60s before each crash to identify the probing source; correlate with UC1's vulnerable-version list to find any host that hasn't yet been patched.
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "nginx" or FileName =~ "nginx"
| where ActionType in ("ProcessCreated","ProcessCreatedUsingWmiCommand")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("worker process","-s reload","master process")
| summarize WorkerRespawns = count(), StartTime = min(Timestamp), EndTime = max(Timestamp) by DeviceId, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, WindowMinutes)
| where WorkerRespawns >= 5     // 5 = empirical worker-respawn floor; healthy nginx restarts cluster on reload, exploit-driven crashes spread over time
| order by WorkerRespawns desc
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ProcessName == "nginx" or SyslogMessage has "nginx"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("worker process", "exited on signal", "SIGSEGV", "SIGABRT", "signal 11", "signal 6")
| extend Signal = extract(@"exited on signal\s+(\d+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| summarize Crashes = count(), Signals = make_set(Signal, 10), Sample = any(SyslogMessage), StartTime = min(TimeGenerated), EndTime = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, HostIP, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMinutes)
| where Crashes >= 3     // 3 = abnormal crash floor per 10m bucket; healthy reloads don't emit SIGSEGV
| order by Crashes desc

Oversized HTTP request headers against NGINX (CVE-2026-42055 trigger condition) AIExploitation Medium
F5's mitigation for CVE-2026-42055 is to reduce `large_client_header_buffers` below 2 MB and drop `ignore_invalid_headers off` — the bug is triggered by malformed/oversized headers reaching the proxy_v2 / gRPC path. Hunt for inbound requests with abnormally large header payloads landing on NGINX-fronted services. Rationale: Article's explicit workaround for CVE-2026-42055 — "reducing the large_client_header_buffers directive size below 2 megabytes" — is the exact trigger condition. NGINX's own error.log emits canonical strings ("client sent too long header line") whenever a request crosses that buffer threshold, so we use those strings + the 2 MB boundary as the hunt anchor.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit clients with overstuffed Cookie / Authorization headers (huge JWTs, SAML assertions)
  • Long Referer chains from analytics-heavy apps
  • Buggy mobile SDKs emitting duplicate headers
  • API gateways forwarding upstream traceparent stacks
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending request line — if header bytes are >2 MB or the error.log says "client sent too long header line" repeatedly from the same source, treat as probing for CVE-2026-42055. 2) Contain: apply the F5-recommended mitigations (remove `ignore_invalid_headers off`; reduce `large_client_header_buffers` below 2 MB) and add a WAF rule blocking total header size >1 MB from the offending ASN. 3) Hunt: correlate the source IPs with UC2 worker-crash events on the same destination host within 60 seconds; check whether the host appears in UC1's vulnerable-build list.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where DeviceProduct has_any ("NGINX", "NGINX Plus", "NGINX Gateway Fabric")
   or DestinationServiceName has "nginx"
| where RequestClientApplication != ""
| extend ReqHeaderBytes = toint(coalesce(DeviceCustomString1, "0"))     // map your CEF custom field for header size
| where ReqHeaderBytes >= 2097152     // 2 MB — F5 mitigation says drop large_client_header_buffers below 2 MB
   or Message has_any ("client sent too long header line", "client sent invalid header line", "upstream sent invalid header")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, ReqHeaderBytes, Message
| summarize Hits = count(), arg_min(TimeGenerated, *) by SourceIP, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct
| where Hits >= 3
| order by Hits desc

NGINX Gateway Fabric arbitrary directive injection (CVE-2026-11311 / CVE-2026-50107) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Both Gateway Fabric flaws let an authenticated attacker inject arbitrary NGINX configuration directives. Hunt for authenticated API/CRD writes that introduce raw nginx config snippets — `proxy_pass`, `server`, `listen`, `lua_*`, `auth_request` — outside expected change windows. Rationale: Article calls out CVE-2026-11311 and CVE-2026-50107 as authenticated injection of arbitrary NGINX directives into Gateway Fabric. Detection pivots on raw nginx-grammar strings (proxy_pass / lua_ / auth_request / listen) appearing inside a Kubernetes CRD update or a config-file write that didn't come from a package manager or known config-management tooling.
ATT&CKT1505.004 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit GitOps/Argo or Flux reconciler pushing CRD updates
  • Operator-team troubleshooting a routing problem via kubectl edit
  • Helm upgrade rendering new Gateway Fabric resources after chart bump
  • Custom internal controllers that inject snippets via supported annotations
Suppression filter
| where Username !startswith "system:serviceaccount:argocd:" and Username !startswith "system:serviceaccount:flux-system:"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RequestObject / file diff — confirm whether the injected text contains raw nginx directives outside the documented Gateway Fabric CRD surface (e.g. inline `lua_` or `proxy_pass` blocks). Identify the authenticated principal (Username / ServiceAccount) and check whether they belong to an approved GitOps controller. 2) Contain: revert the CRD to the prior generation (`kubectl rollout undo` / re-apply from git), rotate the service-account token if the principal is not an expected automation account, and tighten Gateway Fabric RBAC to the minimum set of CRDs. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same principal for prior writes against any Gateway Fabric CRD over the last 30 days, check NGINX error.log on the data-plane pods for unexpected `lua_*` or `proxy_pass` reload messages, and ensure the cluster's Gateway Fabric is patched against CVE-2026-11311 and CVE-2026-50107.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/nginx/", "/etc/nginx-gateway/", "/usr/local/nginx/conf/", "/etc/nginx/conf.d/")
| where FileName endswith ".conf" or FileName == "nginx.conf"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg","rpm","apt","yum","dnf","ansible-playbook","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion","helm","kubectl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where ObjectRef has_any ("gateway.networking.k8s.io", "gateway.nginx.org", "nginxgateways", "nginxproxies", "clientsettingspolicies", "observabilitypolicies")

| where RawObj has_any ("proxy_pass", "lua_", "auth_request", "add_header", "if (", "return 302", "return 301", "rewrite ", "listen ", "include /")
| project TimeGenerated, Username, UserAgent, Verb, ObjectRef, ResponseStatus, RequestUri, RawObj
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc
